THE undersigned, actuated the momentous and þÿ lasting influence the des- by conviction a on of tinies of these Colonies and may be principally of this Island, which the first Colonial Assembly will exercise, that Assembly most likely having to discuss Drafts of Laws respecting Exercise of Trail Mercan- þÿ , tile and Mechanical, þÿ Relations of Masters and Servants, of Planters and Laborers, þÿ Vagrancy, þÿ and in fact nearly all the relations that will more or less influence the well-being of the community and of the individual members of the sameþÿ have thought it their duty to consider the means of best securing a free and effective exercise of the right of vote granted to the inhabitants by the Colonial Law. It is at once obvious, that no beneficial result can be obtained, if the qualifications of the individuals to be voted for are not discussed by the voters, and it is likewise obvious, that such discussion will be very unsatisfactory, if it be restrictf.d to the private circle of each voter. Tlie consequence of such an unsatisfactory discussion may be either that voters will vote at random, or from a caprice, or that they, will from diffidence or other motives less creditable stay away from the voting. Both results we would consider very lamentable and derogatory to the dearest interests of the inhabitants, and at the same time an opprobrium on the voters. We have considered a trial- 'lection by ballot the best means of obviating these evils. Such ballot, if generally attended to, will give voters an opportunity

of finding out the general feeling in the District in regard to such individuals, that may be proposed. When the result of the ballot is made known, wo would consider it a matter of course, that only such individuals as have by the trial-voting obtain 'd a reasonable number of votes should be voted 1 >r at the actual election. Thus canvassing for votes would reasonably be limited to such individuals that according to the trialvoting could be considered to have a chance, and the voters would avoid the disagreeableness to be called upon for votes by individuals whom they of themselves would not think of voting for, a consideration of some moment in a community, where a considerable part of the voters would be more or less dependent on employers or customers, relations that ought not to influence the voting. We therefore invite voters residing in the jurisdictions of Christiansted and Frederiksted to assemble in the respective districts at a time and at places to be advertised, when the lists of voters are ready, in order to ballot for five members of the Colonial Council for Basin and three for Western), the numbers to be voted for in the respective districts. It is to be remarked, that voters from any district may be elected. A Committee of the undersigned will be present to register the voles, the result of which will be made publicly known on the spot and in the St. Croix Avis. St. Croix, Christiansted 28th June 1852. A series of military fetes and banquets have been given by the King of Prussia to the Emperor of Russia and his suite, who are at present visiting various localities in Germany. On the 19th instant evolutions on a grand scale were performed by the Infantry, anti on the 21st by the Cavalry at Berlin, on the Tempelhofer Feld. On the former day the troops were all on the ground and in position before ten þÿo clock General von Wrangel commanded. The regiments reviewed were the 1st and 2nd Foot Guards; the Emperor Alexander Infantry; the Emperor Francis Grenadiers; the reserve Infantry of the Guard; the training battalion of Infantry ; a battalion of Chasseurs of the Guard; a battalion of Rifles of the Guard ; the Pioneers of the Guard; the 8th Infantry Regiment of the Line; the 24th of the Line ; eight

batteries of the Guard Artillery: the above formed the first division. The second was composed of cavalry, and included a regiment of Dragoons of the Guard, the Hussars of the Guard, the Third Hussars (the King of Hanover's regiment), the regiment of Body Guards, the regiment of Cuirassiers of the Guard, the Gilt regiment of Cuirassiers of the Guard (the Emperor of þÿRussia s, and of which his Imperial Majesty wore the uniform, white, with breast-plate, helmet clumsy trick, attempted to be played us? and eagle); the first Uhlans (Lancers) of the Guard ; the 2d Lancers; the 3d Lanþÿ They cers (the regiment of the Hereditary Grand Duke of Russia); and three batteries of horse artillery of the Guards. There were, besides, a corps of cadets, and a great number of old officers þÿ unþÿattached, hut who attended as spectators. The number of troops on the ground was neatly 25,000, hut five times the number might be manoeuvred on the plain with ease. The Emperor of Russia and the King of Prussia, attended by the numerous princely and ducal guests who had come to lterlin to assist at the spectacle, arrived at a quarter to eleven. The cavalcade was magnificent ; the Imperial and Royal staff and the suites numbered 500 horsemen, an irregular mass, of every conceivable uniform, galloping down the immense line of front. They were received by Royal salutes from the batteries, a roll from all the drums, and the strains of die Russian hymn from the regimental hands. The first arrival ol their Majesties was by tar

the grandest moment of the spectacle. The Empress of Russia and the Queen of Prussia, with their suites, followed; their Majesties were in a carriage and eight. As soon as the Emperor had ridden down the lines, and returned to the centre, the troops began to tile past in companies and squadrons, then in column, the cavalry the second time at full trot. 'Flic Emperor placed himself at the head of his Cuirassies Regiment, and led it past the King of Prussia, as if on duty for the day. The troops were in motion for two hours and a half. The Emperor delighted the Prussian officers ot the army by addressing them on his arrival at Potsdam as þÿ his brave comþÿrades, and assuring them þÿ thathis whole heart was with them during a critical þÿperiod. The address was somewhat broken, and did not appear to have been meditated. The officers, on the announcement of the þÿEmperor arrival, s waited on him, and he descended from the balcony of the palace to the staircase peror, to he among you once more. to meet them. þÿ þÿ I þÿrejoice, said the Em- You know me, and you know 1 have always been your true comrade. My whole heart was with you at a critical þÿperiod. (Here the Emperor pressed the hand of Colonel Count von Blumentlial, Commander of the 1st Regiment of the Guard.) þÿ You have maintained your renown; you have remained faithful as you have always been. 1 come to you, an old friend to his old acquaintance. We will always remain friends, and stand firmly by one another as comrades

should ! Will you do þÿthat? There was a general shout of þÿ We will, your Maþÿjesty; on which the Emperor replied, þÿ So it shall be then; friends and comrades let us remain þÿ! On the 21st the evolutions consisted of the repulse of an enemy supposed to be advancing on Berlin from Tempelhof. An engagement of cavalry, followed up by artillery, which opened a heavy fire on the enemy, was among the displays. The foe having been duly driven in upon his first position, the manoeuvres termin ated. In the evening his Prussian Majesty gave a grand banquet in the White-hall of the Palare. Covers were laid for 4GO

persons. The Empress of Russia was too unwell to attend it, but the Emperor, the Princes of the Prussian Royal family, the Prince and Princess of the Netherlands, the Duke and Duchess of Mecklenburg-Strelilz, the Grand Duke and Duchess of Oldenburg, Prince Christian of Gliicksburg, and the Grand Duke of Mecklenburg-Schwerin, were present ; the Ministers of State, the Foreign Ambassadors, the Generals of the district and garrison, and all the officers of the stall' and adjutants, were invited. The Russian Imperial Chancellor, Count Nesselrode, sat opposite the Emperor and the King of Prussia, between the President of the Cabinet, M. von Manteuffel, and General von Wrangel, whose next neighbour was Count Orloff, the Russian Minister of Police. During dinner, the King himself called on the guests to fill their glasses to the brim (bis zum Ramie), and gave the following toast : þÿ þÿ In my own name and that of my army, and in the name of all true Prussian hearts, I give the health of his Imperial Majesty of Russia! God preserve him to that portion of the world which God has given him for an inheritance, and to this age, to which he is þÿindispensable. The Emperor replied, þÿ Dieu conserve rotre þÿMajeste; adding immediately af- terwards in German þÿ þÿ I drink to the welfare of the King of Prussia and his admirable þÿarmy. The political Exiles of 1818. The Galway Vindicator publishes a letter from one of the misguided persons who figured in the year of turbulence, 1848. The writer is Mr. William P. Dowling, a young artist, who resided in London, and took an active part in the Chartist demonstrations of þÿ 48. He was transported to Van þÿDiemen Land, s under the act which prohibited open and advised speaking. Of his companions m exile he says : þÿ þÿ Cutty is working at bis trade, which, until lately, was not very brisk; but the recent gold discoveries in the neighbouring continent has made every trade good now; he is much respected as a sober and industrious man. Fay has always been in constant employment, and he is considered the best workman in the colony. Lacey has opened a shop in Launceston, his wife and five children have come to him, and lie is in a lair way of reaping a fortune, having a great number of men employed, and, particularly since the gold discoveries, has received more orders than he can procure men to execute. Ritchie lias not been very fortunate, but is now in employment. With respect to the country Chartists, none of them have been able to get employment at their trades, there being no factories of any consequence in the colony; they are, however, employed somewhere in the interior as gardeners &.c. Smith þÿO lirien, since his acceptance of a ticket of leave, has lived in great privacy and retirement in the Vale of Avoca, having, in order to employ his highly cultivated mind, con-

descended to become tutor to the young sons of an eminent Irish physician who resides in that retired place. His constant and dignified demeanour has procured him the respect of all, even of those most opposed to him in principles and politics. He is now, I am informed, in very bad health; so much so, that he has been obliged to give up the employment he had accepted, and has got permission to reside in a different locality. Mitchel has been joinpd by his wife and family ; and with such a family, and with he society of his old and exrcilent friend, Mr. John Martin, he must be as happy

Ji © I A T a 3 as it is possible for an exiled rebel to be. þÿO Meagher still resides in his solitary domicile at Lake Sorell, save that the solitude is now somewhat disturbed by the presence of his amiable and beautiful bride. þÿO Donohoeis at present in this town, and has just completed a history of his persecutions in this colony, which would be published immediately, but, in consequence of the gold discovery, printers cannot be procured at any price þÿ they are all gone to the diggings. He purposes to have it, published in Dublin and London for the benefit of his family, as well as in the colonies and America. Letters have been received here from þÿM Manus, enclosing his business cards to his friends þÿ among others, to the Governor and the Comptroller-General. þÿO Doherty is practising his profession at Hobart Town, and is universally respected. When last I had the pleasure of seeing him he was in excellent þÿhealth.

Tlie West India flail Steamers. An important acceleration of the West India mail service lias just been provided for by the issue of new time tables, to go into effect on and after June 2nd. The mail steamers are to sail from Southampton on the 2nd and 17th of each month, and will be due at the same port on the 1st and 16th. The Gulfof Mexico route is to be performed once a month via Havana, instead of by way of Jamaica, as at present. The principal feature in the alteration is an avoidance of delay at St. Thomas. The voyage to Havana from Southampton will occupy twenty days, to Vera Cruz twenty-five days and a quarter þÿ the course of post with Vera Cruz being fifty-nine days. The route to Jamaica will be by a branch steamer, twice a month from St. Thomas, touching at Porto Rico and Jacmel both ways þÿ the course of post from England being forty-four days. The Honduras mail will be despatched from Jamaica, and the Barbadoes, Demerara and Trinidad routes will be performed twice a month by branch packets. The rapidity of the American steamers, by which correspondence could anticipate the English mails, has been the immediate cause of these newr arrangements. þÿ New York lieraid, May 21.

From the New York Star, June, 7. THE DEMOCRATIC þÿNOMINATION THE HON. FRANKLIN PIERCE, OF NEW HAMPSHIRE, FOR PRESIDENT. Well, the þÿ agony, at length, is over. The nomination is made, and the lion. Franklin Pierce, of New Hampshire, is the democratic condidute for the Presidency in 1852. It was found impossible lo harmonize the views of delegates from opposing sections of the Union by the nomination of any one of the candidates most prominently brought forward for the occasion. The friends of Cass were disinclined to go for Huchanan, and the fiiends of Huchanan, were disinclined to go for (hiss, wlule t tie disinclination was naturally inoiensed on each succeeding ballot, by then mutual and doieimined antagonism Both, however, were equally opposed to Judge Douglas, which opposition was cordially reciprocated.
We should be dishonest were we to say that vr« felt, at first, no unpleasant feeling on

the announcement of this nomination. We should be equally dishonest to say that w« were not, at the next moment, gratified It was a consolation to know that, if Mr. Buchanan could not sufficiently harmonize the prepossessions of the delegates, it had at least been done by one, in every respect entitled to the confidence of the Demoratic partv þÿ bv a sound and sterling democrat, a man of splendid talents, a safe and prudent statesman, a gallant soldier, an honest legislator, and a modest, amiable citizen. We had hoped to see Mr. Buchanan fairly placed before the people, for we adorned Ins brilliant intellect and experience, and felt convinced that we could elect him to the Presidency. But as good patriots, and true democrats, it is both our duty and our pleasure to submit to the will of the majority ; and we do it with especial cordiality in view of a candidate, who, like Franklin Pierce, presents us with so many political features to command our admiration, and literally not one for us to condemn. This is the Franklin Pierce who is now the standard bearer of the democratic phalanx for the coming Presidential contest. The whig press will, of course, now pour out their vials of abuse upon his head, nnd no amount of falsehood and misrepresentation will be withheld by them, to prove that he is everything that is imbecile and unworthy. The abolition newspapers commenced this species of warfare the moment they obtained the intelligence of his nomination, for he is known to be utterly hostile to the further agitation

of the slavery excitement, and firmly opposed to every attempt to array one section of the country against another. It is nothing against General Pierce that he did not seek this nomination, and thnt except, when his country called him to the camp, he has always preferred the unobtrusive walks of private life to the turmoils and intrigues of public station. On the contrary, his taste and feelings in this way do him great credit. He will, doubtless, accept the nomination ; and then it will be for the American people to show their appreciation of his modest merit þÿ it will be for them to prove how much more they admire this kind of honest self distrust, than all the disgusting egotism, complacency, and þÿ fuss and feathers' of demagogues whose impudent ignorance, as ' fools rush in where angels fear to tread." induces them to endeavour to throw themselves headlong into positions that solid learning and sound sense cannot but view with proper timidity and profound respect. The rejoicing with which General Pierce's nomination has been received, all over the country þÿ for the telegraph is laden with the accounts of the firing of cannon and other popular demonstrations of satisfaction þÿ convinces us that the convention has acted wisely in his selection The unanimity with which all classes of democrats throw aside their former preferences, and concur in yielding him their hearty support, promises everything in the way of encouragement. If the democracy of the Union give a pull, a strong þÿ

pull, and a pull altogether" lor a nomine that is unobjectionable in any section, he cannot but succeed; and wc feel the most sanguine hope, therefore, thnt our next President of the United States will be the gallant soldier, the learned Senator, the modest citizen, Franklin Pierce, of Goficord, New Hampshire.

New York Weekly Herald, June 8, 1852. Great Fire in Montreal. DESTRUCTION OF OVER A MILLION DOL- LARS WORTH OF þÿPROPERTY LOSS OF LIFE, ETC. Montreal, June 7, 1852. We were yesterday visited with a most destructive conflagration, which has laid in ashes a considerable number of buildings in the business part of the city. The fire commenced at six o'clock, A. M., at the corner of St. Peter and Lemoine streets, in the carpenter shop of J. Martin, which, together with his residence, was quickly consumed, and two ot his children were burned to death þÿ one died on the spot, and the other in the course of the afternoon. From this point the fire extended to old St. Andrew's church, which together with the dwelling-house of J. Mahoney, and several outbuildings, was destroyed. On the opposite side of the street, the store of Kvan Brothers & Co., and No. 21, warehouse, were burned down with a large quantity of valuable goods in them. Other buildings in the neighborhood, including those of Stephan G. Mills, Torrance & Busteed, J. & J. Mitchell, and Lewis &. Levine's Exchange Hotel, were in great danger, and were saved only by the most strenuous exertions of the firemen. A strong wind from the southwest carried the devouring element to St. þÿI aul street, s destroying in its passage the roofs of two houses in St. Francis Xavier street, belonging to Mr. Dewitt, and occupied as exchange offices. The Commercial Buildings, occupied by the imperial customs department, and others, were also consumed, also the store of Seymour &

Whiting, and some outbuildings of Frolhingham <fc Workman, but their store was saved. The fire then extended its ravages on both sides of the street, us far down as Little St. Joseph street, where it was subdued. Several houses facing the steamboat landings were consumed. Total loss estimated at £250,000 to £300,000.

Arrival of Kossuth in IVew York. Kossuth arrived in this city at half past 4 o'clock yesterday afternoon, from Albany. He came down the river in the steamboat Alida. As she neared her dock, Mr. Kossuth and Mrs Kossuth were seen walking on the promenade deck, with four other Hungarians. When the Alida reached the wharf the party immediately came on shore, got into the Irving House carriage, and proceeded to that hotel, where Kossuth went up stairs to his rooms. With the exception of Mr. Tom Bunting, one of our corps of military reporters, there was not a single person on the pier to see the great Hungarian and bid him welcome. Thus it appears that the New York Herald was the only establishment in town that sent a delegation to receive him on his return from his Eastern and Northwestern tour. Where are the hundred of thousands that welcomed him on a previous occasion? He was visited in the course of the evening by Governor Wood, of Ohio, and some other gentlemen staying at the Irving House. But there appeared to be an absence of all fuss or pomp and everything was quite different from his first appearance here. There is no more notice taken of him now than of any private man. He is accompanied by hi secretary, M. Pulasky, and other

St. Thomas Times, 8th May 1852. FOR THE ST. THOMAS TIMES. A Bill for Compensation to the late Owners of Slaves in the Danish West India Possessions. ( Continued from, our last.) When the honorable member in the second place asserts that tlu emancipation was not the result of the individual Act (the Rescript of 28th July, 1847), on which the late slave-owners have founded their right to compensation, we agree with him in the main. In the Regulations of 3rd February, 1755, providing principally for the religious instruction of the slaves; in the ever-memorable Royal Ordinance ol 16th March, 1792, abolishing the slave-trade; in the Royal Ordinance of 1st May, 1840, ameliorating the physical and moral condition of the unfree ; in short, in all the slave-acts which have emanated from the Mother-Country, from the first mentioned Regulations to the Royal Rescript of 28th July, 1847, we more or less perceive the laudable intention ofthe state to liberate theslaves in the colonies. But this circumstance witnesses directly in our favor. All those acts gave us every reason to expect that it was the no less laudable intention of the state to grant compensation whenever the emancipation-act was decreed. The very fact of the emancipation being deferred would roves that the state from time to time not liberate C efore it could comoensate. Not one of those acts even hints that no compensation would be -given. No, not one! The Royal Rescript of 28th July, 1847, distinctly states that the the would not take place ere emancipation expiration

of twelve years, in order that the interests of all parties could be provided for , conse- þÿ quently the interest of the slave-owner included; and in what else could this peculiarly consist but in indemnity for the intended expropriation? But when the honorable member further asserts that slavery in these Islands, after the publication of the Royal Rescript, of 28th July, 1847, was nothing more than domestic servitude, we must confess that we are astounded. The Rescript bears on the very face of it the most unqualified contradiction to his assertion. It is therein most especially stated that slavery shall cease after the expiration of twelve years from the date ofthe Rescript, but in the meanwhile the existing, relations shall remain unimpaired. Now these relations both de facto and de jure remained in full force and vigor up to the day ofthe emancipation. Estates belonging to the Crown, with all the slaves thereon, were sold at public auction in the latter part of 1847. Slaves were bought and sold until the emancipation took place. Nor is the honorable gentleman more fortunate in comparing the state of our lave population at that period to that of the apprenticed labourers in the British colonies. The contrast is so very striking that we are at a loss to account for bis misconstruction. The British Emancipation Act of 28th August, 1833, defined slavery to be extinct ; the Danish Royal Rescript, that slavery would continue for 12 years longer. The British act made it felony

to sell one of the apprenticed labourers. The Danish Rescript permitted the sale ofthe unfree, although promised liberty within a specified time. The 38th section ofthe slave regulations, bearing date the 3rd February, 1755, in which it was explicitly laid down as law that slaves were part and parcel of property, was fully confirmed by the Royal Rescript of 28th July, 1847, for it declared that the heretofore existing relations remained intact. | by the emancipation having taken place The British apprenticed the labourers

3 Wo ® Ifc A T 11 for 6 years þÿ their services could be transferred for the benefit of the owners, and England yet compensated the proprietors liberally in money. We demand only the latter! The question of indemnity to the late slave-owners is strictly colonial, says the honorable member. How can he make this agree with his preceding assertion, that the state during a series of years has steadily carried out its plan of emancipating the slaves in these Islands, we cannot conceive. The inconsistency becomes greater, if possible, when we call to mind that the honorable gentleman as a member of the States-General is fully aware that the inhabitants of the Mother Country, in the year 1844, and afterwards, petitioned the states for the abolition of slavery in the Danish West India Islands; and, in consequence thereof, the states not only recommended the prayers of the petitioners to our late þÿSovereign s most gracious consideration, but most submissively solicited that a draft of a j bill for emancipation should he laid before them for the purpose of eliciting their opinion and advice on the subject. Was this done at the instance of the colonists? Not at all ! Were the colonists represented in the States-General? Not at all ! And in what did the proceedings ofthe states result? In the Rescript of the 28th July, 1847, which, like all half I measures, has proved disastrous in the extreme to the proprietors, and will eventually become so to the laborers unless compensation is granted. It is

thus evident that the question of the emancipation was mooted in the Mother Country, at the instance of her inhabitants; that it was effected by her legislators, and sanctioned by the Home-Government. The inhabitants of the Mother Country are, therefore, bound in honor, inequity, injustice, to compensate us for the losses sustained through their delibt rate acts Let it, however, be granted that the matter in all its bearings is entirely colonial. Could this circumstance exonerate the inhabitants of the Mother Country from helping us, when brought to a state from which to irretrievable ruin there is but a step? And this after having for a number of years reaped all advantages from the colonies? The matter is colonial ! so is the war at the Cape of Good Hope, occasioned by the colonists having extended the limits of their original settlements into the interior of the country. Notwithstanding the Cape-colonists strenuously opposed the measures of Eng- | land with regard to the convicts question, ; she has yet voted several millions to carry on the war. And shall we, who are guiltless in every respect, who have always submitted to the will ofthe parent state, be suffered to sink under our difficulties þÿ to perish for our loyalty! Oppose not the passing of the Bill, unless you will doom the planters and their families, the widows, orphans and minors, to a worse state of penury and want þÿ the laborers to that of ignorance j and barbarism. Every opposition to the

measure accelerates the ruin of all ! And let it not be said that the philantropists of the mother Country would vie with those of Great Britain, Sweden and France, at the expense of the slaveowners in these Islands. The last opponent to the Bill, the honorable Mr. Ilothe, grounds his objections on this proposition, that, from the gradual decrease ofthe slave population anterior to the emancipation, it must be inferred that their number would have sunk from 21,000 to 12,000. Ergo, says this þÿ subtile þÿexperimentalist, the late slave-owners have gained considerably
in 1848, or eleven years sooner than de-

fined by the Royal Rescript of 28th July, 1847. If we were disposed to admit the correctness of his premises, we would yet be obliged to reject his conclusion. He himself does not admit either. This is evident, as be afterwards as serts, that the desire of being liberated would have induced many ofthe unfree, in the course of time, to purchase their freedom; and the price of an unfree would have declined in the same ratio as the term of the final emancipation advanced. The 9,000 unfree, consequently, would have paid for their manumission; and the other 12,000 would, during the 12 years fixed by the Royal Rescript, have labored steadily, without pecuniary remuneration from their owners, who also otherwise could have disposed of their services to advantage. Besides, at the expiration of that period, the owners then would have been as much entitled to compensation from the state as they are now. Their claims would not have been one jot less sacred. This opinion they þÿ for have in fact always entertained , they would not suppose an imposþÿsibility. The state of things after the publication of the Royal Rescript was not such as the honorable speaker depicts it; for it cannot rationally be fancied that anv planter possessing common sense would liave then purchased slaves as part and parcel of estates, at very high prices. It may be fancied as an experiment. But the matter is of too much vital importance to innumerable individuals to bear experiments. A few words at parting, for the pre-

sent, with our honorable friends, the opponents ol the Bill þÿ we will not call them enemies. We respect their motives. They have erred in their opinions on men and thing in the colonies, because they have no; been thoroughly enlightened on the subject. Nay, we can even forgive Messrs. Jespersen and Winther for their immatured notions, and erroneous estimation of us, expressed on another occasion. We have known persons even in the Colonies who, having skimmed the surface of things here, fancied they had fathomed the depth; and, therefore, communicated like absurd, ridiculous and puerile ideas to their friends and connexions on that side ofthe Atlantic. Let us, however, pay unto the opponents of the Bill the homage of firmly believingthat, properly enlightened, they will, as in all other instances, not fail to render justice where it is certainly due. The Observer , April II. 1852 F IS \ \ þÿ E. ¬ It was rumoured in the lobbies of the Chamber that the session would not last more than a month, and that the deputies would adjourn for want of oceupation. The general opinion among political men in Paris is that the proclamation ot the empire will take place in a very short time. Public rumour has fixed on tin 5th of May for that purpose. On that day a great review is to take place on the Place de Carrousel, at which it is calculated that nearly 150,000 men, including the regular troops and the National Guards, w ill be prese nt. It is said that on that occasion the troops will be encouraged to salute the Emperor with their acclamations, and that a pfeliseih will immediately afterwards be submitted to the people, asking the opinion of France on the subject. Similar rumours have been current on former occasions, which led to nothing; but it must be said that the probability of their being right was never greater than now. Every day something or other occurs to show bow the ideas of people in high places are þÿ still þÿharping on the empire. It is remarked, for instance, that the ribbon of the new medal, instituted by Louis Napoleon out of the spoils ot the House of Orleans, is the ribbon of the order of the Iron Crown, and that the medal is surmounted by the crown of Italy, as in the time of the great Napoleon. It is also said that Prince Lucien Murat has begun to put forth his pretensions to the crow n of Naples ; and he has recently exposed himself to some ridicule by going

to the ceremony of the opening of the assembly in a carriage with the arms ot Naples emblazoned upon it. A reported interview at Aix-la-Cha pelle between the Duke þÿd Aumale and Generals Cliangarnier and Lamoriciere, on the return of the duke from Italy to England þÿ lias contributed, not perhaps to exite alarm, but certainly to annoy
the French Government; and as it seldom happens that one trouble comes alone, the death of Prince Sehwarzenberg has increased their dissatisfaction.

Among the powers said to be most hostile to the re-establislmient of the empire, is undoubtedly Russia. The list of the senators who are to receive salaries has at last been decided on. Elie de Beaumont, and M. Dumas. Almost all the generals are salaried. The Court of Tuscany, emboldened by (lie advent of a Tory Cabinet, has peremptorily refused to admit for the claim preferred by Lord Granville apology and compensation in the case of Mr. Erskine Mather. A gross outrage has been committed on an Englishman, and now, doubtless, at the instigation of þÿ our oldest þÿally, Austria, and relying probably upon the presumed indifference of Lord þÿGranville successor, s the Tuscan Government refuses to redress one of the foulest wrongs. On the 29th of January Mr. Erskine Mather, walking arm-in-arm with his brother in one of the narrow streets of Florence, encumbered at the moment by a crowd following a military band, felt himself struck from behind with the flat edge of a sword. Turning round to remonstrate, he received a blow in the face with a fist from a person in the dress of an Austrian officer. Mechanically raising his arm to protect himself, he was at once cut down by the officer ill command of the detachment by which the band was accompanied. The sword of the officer passed through a thick felt hat, and inflicted a deep wound, two inches in length, on the upper part of his forehead. Mr. Mather, covered with blood, was assisted by (lie passengers to a neighbouring hospital, where he was confined for three weeks, and where, after the first few days, no one hut his brother was permitted to see him without an order from the police. The hone havingbeen seriously injured, the wound, after healing rapidly on the surface, had
to be re-opened to admit of suppuration Inflammation ensuing,

hied in the arm, and once in the hand At length, the shadow of his former self, and with a constitution irreparably weakened for life, lie recovered sufficiently to be carried to bis lodgings. The Sierra Nevada brings us news from Kingston, Jamaica, to the 10th inst. The intelligence from the island is embraced in the letter of our Kingston correspondent : þÿ Our Jamaica Correspondence. Kingston, Ja., April 9 0 I. M. þÿ The Sierra Nevada's Passengers þÿ The Weather þÿ The Distress of the Country The Public Health. But for the arrival here to-day of the magnificent Sierra Nevada, Kingston would he dressed in her Sunday garb

this being Good Friday. As it is, there is a little life infused into things by your lively countrymen, who are taking their walks to and fro, attracting, as they generally do, swarms of little urchins, who are anxious to show the good hearted travellers any and every thing þÿ of course for a consideration. Many a dollar i parted with under these circumstances. The weather here þÿ I speak of Kingston, Spanish Town, and their immediate vicinities þÿ has become very warm. The mountainous districts are unusually pleasant, and to one not acquainted with locality in this country, it would become exceedingly strange how so sensible a change of climate could he felt in a few hours. Had we railroads up the mountains, we might move the heat of summer to at least the mildness of winter in about one hour. The only thing agitating the public at this moment þÿ and very naturally so, too þÿ is the alarming distress of the country. The shoe has now began to pinch every one þÿ laborer, mechanic, planter, merchant þÿ all alike are suffering from the same cause ; and unless the protecting arm of England, or some other friendly power, is stretched forth to raise us, we are, indeed, doomed. Some parties are in high feather at the change of ministry in England, which will, no doubt, he of benefit to us if they are able to retain their places; but, anxious as 1 should þÿ be to see this, 1 fear the old saying þÿ the thing is too good to þÿlast. Memorials are being sent home from all quar-

j ters of the country, and delegates will leave in the first English steamer, to represent our cause at home. For a place like this, there never was more party feeling than has cursed this country ; but yet 1 am happy to say, on the subject of our distress, and the cause of it, there is an entire oneness of feeling. Sincerely do I hope, for the honor of England þÿ for the sake of her consistency, and for the sake of poor Jamaica þÿ j that we shall yet he saved from the late that awaits us. The island is not as healthy as might be desired. There are very many cases of measles in the city, and few cases of small pox. This latter disease is very prevalent on the north side of the island, and 1 trust it will not spread. Vaccination has been very generally taken advantage of, and I trust the rava ges of the destroyer may, in consequence, he arrested. I shall he glad if I am able to acquaint you, in my next, that the enemy has entirely departed.

The llctiirii of the 7Zerlin We announced yesterday the arrival of the British mail steam ship Merlin from Bermuda. It will he recollected that several weeks ago we stated that she struck on a reef off the island of St. Thomas, at midnight, on the 17th ot March, and broke her shaft, which prevented her from getting into port. We now learn that the French government steamer Crocodile, Captain Choux, arrived at St. Thomas on the morning ot the 18th of March, and the French Consul, Mr. Piecione, having informed Captain Choux that the Merlin was off the port disabled, Capt. Choux at once put his ship about without coming to anchor, and proceeded to the Merlin, and towed her into St. Thomas. Too much praise cannot be given to Capt. Choux for his noble conduct on the occasion. The Merlin will sail on her regular day, the 8th of May. þÿ Ibid.
Tlir Irish Emigrant in America. We arc grateful to the Daily Times for its manner of reference to our people; þÿ for its fair and candid and gentlemanly

temper. How easy to tell the man of liberal and refined views and educated training, from the semi-civilised bigot and coarse vulgarian ! If America has a flaw or blot on her magnificent institutions, it is the low ribaldry and bald ignorance of portions of her Press. To be sure they are but exceptions to the general rule, and are quite overshadowed by such generous and gifted þÿ organs of þÿopinion as the Timet. That paper of þÿMonday s date treats of the poor but honest, faithful and affectionate Irish Emigrant þÿ thus : þÿ The Galway Mercury , speaking of the wholesale emigration of the Irish peasantry from that county, remarks that the parties who left within the last two years are now sending home in small former þÿexample. þÿ sums þÿ an amount of money beyond all þÿIdP 11 This is one of the many agencies by which emigration is so rapidly and largely increased. The Irish who come | to this country þÿ especially the younger classes þÿ are generally economical, and manage to save something out of their scanty earnings to send home to assist their parents, brothers, wives or children to follow them to the United States. The amount of money thus remitted every year, is immensely large, and indicates at once the degree of prosperity which the emigrants have met, and their cherished regard for those they have left at home. When we look into our Alins Houses, and other public institutions, or j observe the number of persons crowded into the lodging-houses provided for

emigrants, we are apt to draw very un- j favorable inferences as to the character of that vast multitude of people thrown every year by the waves upon our shores. Hut this is a very unjust judgment, because it denouncesrthe whole on account i of the faults of the few. Compared with the whole number of emigrants, a very small proportion are of the character referred to. The great mass of them are i hard-working, economical and prudent; and the vast sums of money remitted by them every year to their friends at home, peaks volumes in their þÿpraise. The principal cause of introducing the above is to enable us to state a fact honorable to the name of Irishmen, and to human nature. The father of three children þÿ an intelligent and respectable tradesman þÿ had been forced to enter the work-house in a certain town of one of I the midland counties of Ireland. The guardians ot the union perceiving his industrious spirit, and desirous to give him a chance, paid his passage to New York. He came here, obtained employment, saved his earnings, and was soon in a position to send for his beloved family. In doing so lie remitted to the chairman and clerk ol the hoard as much money as covered the expenses of his own support and the support of his children during their stay in the establishment ! Besides; he refunded with gratitude and with interest t he money ad vanced to enable him to emigrate ! That man is now a respectable and prosperous tradesman in this city, and j has iiis adored family about him eating

the sweet and wholesome bread of industry and independence. We do not know what others may think of this incident, but to us it is a noble evidence of the truth and honor of manhood. Emigrants who act thus endorse and justify the generous opinion of such paper as the Times. þÿ The Irish American.

Anecdote. þÿ When Macdonough was first Lieutenant of the Siren, under command of Captain Smith, a circumstance occurred in the harbour of Gibraltar, sufficiently indicative of the firmness and decision of his character. An American merchant brig came to anchor near the United States vessel. Macdonough, in the absence of Capitain Smith, who had gone on shore, saw a boat from a British frigate board the brig and take from her a man ; he instantly manned and armed his gig, and pursued the British boat, which he overtook, just as it reached the frigate, and, without ceremony, took the impressed man into his own boat. The þÿfrigate s boat was twice the force of his own ; but the act was so bold as to astound the Lieutenant who commanded the press gang, and no resistance was offered. When the affair was made known to the British Captain, he came on board the Siren in a great rage, and inquired how he dared to take a man from his boat. Macdonough replied, that the man was an American seaman, and was under the protection of the flag of the United States, and that it was his duty to protect him. The Captain, with a volley of oaths, swore he would bring his frigate alongside the Siren, and sink her. þÿ but while she swims, the man you will þÿ That you may þÿdo, said Macdonough; not þÿhave. The English captain told Macdonough that he was a young hair brained fellow, and would repent of his rashness. þÿ Supposing, þÿsir, said he, þÿ had I been in that boat, would you have dared to have com-

mitted such an þÿact? þÿ I should have made the attempt at all þÿhazards, was the reply. þÿ would you venture to interfere if I þÿ What þÿsir! said the English captain, were to impress men from that þÿbrig? þÿ You can try it, þÿsir, replied Macdonough. The British captain returned to his vessel, manned a boat, and steered for the brig: Macdonough did the same; but here the affair ended ; the English captain took a circuitous route and returned to his ship. New Way to Cure Sick Clerks. þÿ The Dayton Gazette relates the following story of Secretary Corwin. Its humor is characteristic : To a friend of ours who saw him the other day, at Lebanon, he gave a most amusing, and we doubt not the truthful account of the condition of things in the treasury department, when he entered upon the duties of secretary. The clerks, he estimated, were sick, on an average, about half the time þÿ but it struck him as somewhat remarkable, that much as they were sick, none of them died. The fact was apparent at a glance, that they did very little work for the public, and the inference was irresistible, that something must be done for them. Accordingly the secretary turned physician, and began prescribe to for the invalids. He issued an order that all clerks who were absent from their desks a certain number of days, say two, on account of sickness, should submit to a proportionate deduction from their respective salaries; and

that all who were absent longer, say one week, should be required either to die or resign. The prescription worked like a charm, and in a short time there was not a sick clerk in the whole department. A healthier set of men than they are now, Mr, Corwin declares cannot be found anyr where.

How to Grow þÿRich. The only way by which capital can increase is by saving. It you spend as much as you get, you will never be richer than you are. Tis not what a man gets, but what he saves, that constitutes his wealth. Go, learn the first two rules of arithmetic : learn addition and substruction. Add to your present capital any amount you please : substract the sum which you add, and tell me if the last amount will not be the same as the first. Every merchant should, in every year of his life, make some addition to his capital. þÿY ou say you get but little ; never mindspend less than that little ; and then next year you will get more, for you will have the profit upon the sum you save. There is no Royal road to wealth any more than to geometry. The man who goes on spending all he gets, and expects that by some lucky hit he shall he raised to wealth, will most likely sink into poverty; for, in case of adverse fortune, he has then no resource; whereas, by economy, he may lay by a stock that may serve as a provision in case of adversity. Y ou may say that the times are bad, tile seasons are bad, the laws are bad. Be it so; hut, were the case reversed, it would make no difference to you. Look at home ; you spend more than you get. How, then, can you be otherwise than poor ? How many a respectable family have fallen from a high station, which they worthily and honourably filled, merely because neither the gentleman nor the lady had been familiar with the first four rules of arithmetic.

The Old Style of Puffing. þÿ The George þÿRobins advertising s was long in the ascendant. It still has its disciples ; but the spirit of the mighty founder has been laid, and his imitators follow at a respectful distance. The/ige of puffing lost a most distinguished champion when that redoubted knight of the hammer was finally removed from the arena of fairy land, in which he so long and so chivalrously fought. At his magic touch, estates became a paradise ; at a wave of his hand, a barren heath was changed into a glowing harvest field. Ponds swelled into lakes; molehills into mountains ; roods and perches struggled into acres ; a clump of trees became metamorphosed into a forest of timber ; a modest dwelling-house was mystically changed into a palace ; a struggling tenantry, amongst whom a lordly purchaser was invited to take up his dwelling, was made to enjoy the perfection of rural bliss þÿ the acme of agricultural prosperity. Rates and taxes vanished at his approach, his and rack-rent fell to zero. The lot of happy peasantries always contrasted favourably with the condition of those in town. His hamlet tasted all the happiness of an Arcadia, and his model communities had long since accomplished the millennium. Common auctioneers consulted Euclid for their measurements þÿ Cocker for their calculations. George Robins invented systems of geometry and arithmetic for himself, which possessed this remarkable virtue þÿ that as he worked the problems and the sums, the result was invariably
in favour of his client. The false critic is the serpent who has stolen into the literary garden. He is the great enemy of knowledge.

The þÿ þÿAVIS. Cliristiansted, Friday the 21st of May 1802. It is with unfeigned gratification we state that the St. Croix Savings Bank will be opened on Saturday th. 29th instant, in an office neatly fitted up for the purpose. under Government House. We have, on many occasions, commented on th utility and practicability of establishing a Saving. Tank in this Island, as it would be the means of inducing the labouring classes to practice economy and industry, and thereby become useful members of the community. Our most sanguine expectations are now realised þÿ the Bank is established, and will be ready to receive deposits in the course of a few (Ihvs. It is now left to the people to avail themselves of the advantages of so excellent an institution those þÿ who take an interest in the prosperity of this Island, and in their own welfare, will know how to appreciate this Institutionsimple-minded persons will, no doubt, view it witii a suspicious eye. This may arise from ignorance of the object of such an institution, and can only be removed by the example of those who become depositors and by the advice of persons in whom they may place confidence. We would therefore respectfully submit this consideration to the clergymen of this Island, whether they cannot be instrumental in explaining to the members of their respective congregations the advantages and security arising from the use of such banks. We wish the Institution every success !

St. Thomas Times, loth May 1852. FOR THE ST. THOMAS TIMES. A Hill for Compensation to the lute Owners of Slaves in the Danish West India Possessions. ( Continued from No. 873. From the opponents of the measure, we turn to its advocate, the honorable Colonel Tscherning. In him we at once perceive the In statesman. gallant soldier and practical him we see fully realised the well grounded anticipation of the petitioners for compensation, that their just cause would not fail -in obtaining strenuous advocates in the Diet. And certainly just cause never had worthier advocate than the gallant Colonel þÿ the þÿpeasant s friend. Whether we examine the mild chastisement inflicted by the honorable Colonel on the honorable member for \eile (Lehmann) :

þÿ But when he says, that which we ought to contribute should he to renounce on the revenues of the colonies in favor of such an arrangement, it unquestionably is a very inconsiderable contribution he thereby promises the colonies (assent), and l am apprehensive, that it is so trifling, that if there he anything owing in the case, it would be a jest to grant that only; hut to scoff at a subject of this nature is a sin or we scrutinize the practical view he takes of the matter ; þÿ We should bear in mind that the colonies have not created the present state of things, but that the Mother Country has been the cause of it. If the Mother Country has occasioned it for her own advantage, the obligation is evident, we owe it ; and if she has done it to her disadvantage, shall the colonies suffer, because our administration has been bad, and to our disadvantage þÿ? we behold the staunch champion of truth and justice, the real philanthropist. Again we find the redoubtable Knight taking the field on the side of justice and equity. þÿ The question, if anything shall be given not will depend on this circum- or stance, whether the force majture which caused the emancipation was so decisive, þÿ that we can screen ourselves behind and say here is nothing to give. This I do not for my part believe we ought quite to þÿdo. Now, if after such substantial proofs of the honorable þÿmember zeal s and interest for our cause, we still differ from him in the following points, we flatter ourselves that he will not attribute it to

want of deference on our part. We owe him much, but we also owe truth and justice more. Ignorance of the facts rendered him feeble. Knowledge of the tacts makes us strong. The honorable colonel declares that he agrees in opinion with the honorable member tor Veile, when he says, that the question of indemnity ought to be referred to the colonies for the purpose of being adjusted there, ere the Diet decides upon the matter. Such a stejr would be tantamount to a rejection of the bill. It would be fruitless, it would be impolitic, it would he destructive. It would be fruitless, inasmuch as the amount, required for the compensation could only be raised by imposing a direct tax on the colonists. But this burden would fall chiefly on the sufferers, the proprietors of lands and houses; for the artizans and laborers have nothing wherewith to pay. It would be impolitic, for whilst the deterioration of the estates mortgaged to the state would in the mean while sink them to insignificance in value no body of men in the colonies could conscientiously fix the rate of the indemnity, which the Mother Country will have to pay, so low as the Government has done. It would be destructive, because every procrastination of the final settlement of the matter only makes bad worse for all parties. The honorable member accounts it a fortunate circumstance for the state, that during 24 hours at least, it was a general wish in the Island (St. Croix) that the emancipation should take place.

It can certainly not reflect dishonor even on a body of soldiers, who, on being surprised by a superior force, retreat for a moment. But when they soon after rally, charge, and overthrow the enemy, their behaviour most undoubtedly deserves reward, but not punishment. So it was with many of the peaceable colonists of St. Croix. And if they did not make the enemy captives of their bows and spears, it was owing to their loyalty to the Sovereign, whose Representative

The Vienna Lloyd contradicts the statement of the Debat that diplomatic conferences are to be held at London on the subject of the Danish succession. The matter, it says, was settled by the five great powers before the Austrian troops evacuated the duchies. The Danish Ministry is engaged in a dispute with the Germanic Diet on the subject of the Holstein federal contingent. The Diet demands that the King of Denmark, as Duke of Holstein, shall bo>d a separate military contingent at its disposal ; and the monarch replies, in very decisive language, that he has as good a right as the Emperor of Austria to keep his army þÿ one and þÿindivisible; and to design to whatever troops he may please to the German service. All he will promise is, that a federal contingent shall remain as a rule in Holstein, and be generally composed of natives of the duchy. The Diet considers that it has made a bad bargain in restoring the sovereign authority without assuring its own influence at the same time.

FRANCE. It appears that it is positively on the 10th May that the grand review for the distribution ol the eagles to the army will take place. The whole of the force quartered in Paris and its neighbourhood will be present, and the other regiments of the army will be represented each by its colonel and a deputation. On the evening of the 9th a fete will be given at the Military School by the army to the President of the Republic, who has signified his acceptance of the invitation ; while, before the ball commences, fireworks, which are in course of preparation by the artillery regiment of Vincennes, will play from the heights of Chaillot, fronting the Champ de Mars. þÿ Coming events cast their shadows before þÿ; certainly all this looks somewhat Imperial. In the meantime one or two organs of the Elysee, rather than of the Government, are growing more Napoleonean perhaps than Napoleon himself. Prince Paul of Wurtemberg, brother of the reigning King of Wurtemberg, brother-in-law of Jerome Bonaparte, and, consequently, uncle of the President, expired on Friday morning, at his hotel in the Place Vendome. It is said that the Prince was converted before his death

from the Protestant faith to Roman Catholicism. This secret death-bed conversion has caused great excitement amongst the family of the Prince. The budget for 1853 shows a deficiency ol 40,000,000 francs, caused by carrying on extraordinary public works. Arrangements were, however, contemplated, which would effect a reduction of 32,000,000 francs, so that no loan would be required. The Moniteur publishes the following communicated note: þÿ A great number of persons imagine and report that the empire is to be proclaimed on the occasion of a fete. To attribute to the Government the desire of the pretext for changing the established order of things is to form a very false idea of the manner in which it understands its duties. If necessity should ever lead to such a resolution it would only be accomplished on the initiative of the constituted powers, and with the consent of the whole people. As to the acclamations of the army, they are, it is true, for the chief ol the state, a valuable proof of the sentiments with which it is animated, but they cannot produce any political result. Thus, at the ceremony of 10th May next, the 60,000 men assembled in the Champ de Mars would in vain salute the President by the name of Emperor, as that act would not advance the re-establishment of the empire one hour. The impression in Paris still remains that the empire is only a question of time. Letters from Havre mention that the Government steamer Berthollet, from Brest, arrived there on the 23rd, for the

purpose of taking on board 371 political prisoners sentenced to transportation by court-martial. The Ministries of the Interior and Police are at present occupied with a matter which stirs great scand I, and will be shortly submitted to the Council of State. The central commissioner of police of one of the chief cities in the south is on the point of being arrested, on the charge of having trafficked in pardons, and sold for hard cash commutations of punishments, or releases from prisons. The fact was denounced to the authorities by a prisoner, who had procured his liberty by this corrupt channel, and has since been confirmed by others. The Debats announces that the government has determined on referring the question of competency, affirmed by the tribunal of the Seine, in the matter of the Orleans property, to the council of state. By this stop the legal tribunals of the country are debarred from interference in the question raised by the state. þÿ Ibid.

To the Editor of the St. Thomas Times. Sir. þÿ In conformity with an advertisement published in the þÿ þÿTidende, calling upon the Electors to assemble on Monday evening last, at the þÿ Bank; for a special purpose that of þÿSavings electing proper members for t lie Colonial Council þÿ at the hour appointed there was a large number assembled, no motion was offered to ascertain who convened the meeting, but Mr. S. Rothschild being called upon to take the Chair, that Gentleman, after little deliberation, proposed that, owing to the crowded state, and insufficient accommodation, that an adjournment should take place, and he proposed it should " be the following evening, at half-past þÿo clock, at the Commercial Hotel, generally known as þÿ þÿBonnelly ; s that being seconded the meeting dispersed without knowing by whom it had been convened ! On Tuesday, a greater number of persons were on the lloor at the appointed place and time, the majority of whom were unprepared to take part in the discussion ; the parties connected with the object of the meeting took care to provide themselves with written statements to carry out their designs, whilst at least two-thirds of the members remained ignorant of their plans, deprived of the same advantage as the sequel will show. Mr. Rothschild was, for a second time, called to the Chair ; and I avail myself of this opportunity to acknowledge the gentlemanly deportment, the calm and patient conduct with which he conduct-

ed the proceedings, as well the good temper with which he received the jovial remarks intended only to relieve the dullness of the evening, approved of by the majority of the company. On the proposal of some member, and at the request of the Chairman, the parties calling the meeting were challenged, when Mr. M. B. Snnmonds approached, and acknowledged it was by himself, Mr. Kierulff, and others; who the others were remains yet to he known. The Chairman then informed the members that the object of the meeting was to secure fit representatives for the Colonial Council. Mr. Rothschild then, in an excellent address, explained to the meeting the extent of its duties, recommending that the members would give their opinion freely. It was generally expected that from those who came forward with written speeches some useful information would he elicited, in place of which all their proposals ended in nothing; one was not even read. Resolutions prematurely concocted were lost by a large majority þÿ the designs of the movers defeated, parties who were unable to obtain any share of popularity towards their being elected þÿ members of the coming Council were floored ! The original object of the meeting was then set aside abruptly, and another proposal made that the voters should bind themselves to a promise in which they will never succeed þÿ that of having our own and separate Council. It only requires reflection, and a correct reading of the Colonial Law, to he convinced
that a divided Council can never be granted. When His Majesty proposed, and the Diet agreed, to adopt the Colonial Law as necessary and indispensable, for the

interests of the Islands, we could not remain insensible to His þÿMajesty s paternal consideration, nor can we withhold our acknowledgment to Count Sponneck, our distinguished Minister for the Colonies, who supported and carried, amidst every obstacle, the lights of these inhabitants of these Islands? Delegates were appointed to represent our interests at St. Croix, to examine and report on laws distinguished for liberality. Such appeared not to have totally answered the views of some þÿ our Commissioners being in the minority, could not accomplish all they wished or laboured for, that particular object being already freely discussed þÿ which you gentlemen will now try by petition. Nevertheless on their return to this Island, the public evinced a general satisfaction, from which it would he inferred that they had performed their duty to their constituents. Was there any fault found to the contrary? No! all wensatisfied. Several months have elapsed, and now we have the announcement (it correct) that our noble Minister had ex pressed his surprise at our having failed to avail ourselves of the whole of the original draft proposed þÿ therefore an important and irretrievable error had been committed. That I did second a motion made by Doctor Pretto, on Tuesday evening last", for a division of the Council was a premature act, and without the reflection necessary at the moment, but after cor. sideration, aware that serious consc quences may be the result, I am led tr

announce it publicly. A petition for a separate Council at this juncture, and previously to allowing a fair trial whereby to ascertain its advantages, or disadvaii tages in my humble opinion will prove in vain. But let whatever the community intend, by petition, go to the Council after it be formed, when the petitioners would perhaps obtain that point which is desired. Under this painful emergency, our best exertions rest in the endeavour to obtain His þÿMajesty approval s that Saint Thomas be appointed as the Head Quarters ot the Danish West India Islands þÿ the only alternative left us to hope that by that the Colonial Council will he permanently fixed. After having said thus much on the subject, and with the hope of obtaining the approval and support of the public, 1 subscribe myself Your obedient servant, J. CAPPE. St. Thomas, 24th June, 1852.

London Times, June 16, 1852. DENMARK. An important measure in reference to the finances of the Duchies of Schleswig and Holstein has just been taken by the Danish Government. By a decision of the Council of State of the 7th inst. Denmark refuses to acknowledge the loans raised and debts contracted by the insurrectionary Governments of 1848 and the following years. All obligation on account of these loans, compulsory or voluntary, on the part of the Treasury of the kingdom, is disavowed. An exception is made for such sums as were deposited in coupons or notes of those loans, as the securities or caution money on the part of officials; when the term of the security ceases, or the caution money is withdrawn, the amounts will lie paid back to the parties at the value at which it was received. In both Houses of Parliament the subject has been discussed, maica have been impressing upon com- ; has staple and, out of doors, deputations from Jamercial gentlemen the absolute necessity of doing something to arrest the ruin of our Sugar Colonies in that part of the world. Plenty of sympathy is felt for the wretched condition of the West Indies, but it is confined to words, þÿ mere lip service ; and, judging from the tone of the head of the Government, the feeling is not likely to show itself in any overt act. Some of the speakers urge, for instance, that, while Government has done so much for the Cape of Good Hope, the extension of pecuniary aid, to meet the state of the West Indies, is justified by the extreme necessity of the case, and that, without some change of a serviceable kind, a revulsion to barbarism is inevitable. Our own feeling is that a loan to the West Indies would not be unpopular, if it were taken up by the Government. It would be found much easier, for instance, to effect a loan than to secure the reintroduction of the differential duties. Respecting the latter, the feeling of the nation would be at once called into play, and interests and parties would be arrayed against the effort against which it would be hopeless

to struggle. If the loan were the means of introducing additional labour and improved machinery into the island, the project would not be unfavourably re- | most occasion, garded by Lord the people Derby at did home. not On this i þÿ come þÿout as lie was expected, and as he ought have done. He seemed deter- to red from touching the subject because of its unpopularity. The fear of the hustings, not the justness or the urgency of the case, evidently restrained him. As far as his Premiership has gone, Lord Derby has not made a very successful leader, lie certainly displayed an absence of tael during the debate in I the peers, relative to the petition of the authorities at Jamaica, which confirms

The occasion was opportune, and another is hardly likely to lie afforded during the remainder of the Session, which is almost certain to terminate in the course of ten days or a fortnight. Instead ot putting the issue on its electioneering phase, it would have been far better to have shown that a grant from the Imperial treasury for the relief of an integral port! he empire, where the elements of s relief be afforded, was not without precedent. In the case of Ireland, when the famine prevailed, relief was prompt ly given to the extent of eight or ten millions, and what was done in the ease of Ireland, critically circumstanced, i equally applicable to the present deplorable condition of the West Indies. The only man in this debate who really seemed to comprehend the subj ject was Lord Grey, and he was so armed

match for the Premier. Our readers that we have always advocated the claims of the West Indies to justice at the hands of the Imperial Government on grounds different in degree to some ol'our friends, but based on reasoning, as we conceive, which is wholly unanswerable. The difficulties of the West Indies arise mainly from two causes, þÿ first, the paucity of labour and its consequent dearness, and secondly, the low range of prices for tropical produce. We do not think that the present prostration is entirely owing to the difference between free and slave labour; and if it were, no remedy need be looked for in that quarter. But more free labour required, and it would be forthcoming it the Government were to set its shoulder resolutely to the task. A liberal grant for this object could not, with any sense of decency, be resisted. Again, the product of the West Indies been going down year after year, and must continue to go down, as the beet root increases in quantity and quality. Now, if the production of sugar at tiie present time does not pay, might not cotton, or some other article largely in demand, be substituted? A ready adaptation of means to an end is as essential to the success of the planter as to that of the merchant, or even the statesman. This is an element in West Indian life which must not be overlooked, and we dwell upon it thus emphati callv, because the fiscal policy of this country seems likely to continue during the present generation in the channel into which it has recently set. No one

The tactics of our public men show that it is so. Every man with a heart in his bosom must be pained to see the present position of West Indian property, and the deplorable state of West Indian society. From being for centuries amongst the most prosperous and the happy of the Colonies of the Crown, they are now almost valueless; and, unless the British Legislature is disposed to 'Xtend to them a helping hand in the hour of need, it would be really better to allow them to make such terms with the Americans, or with' others, as would raise their moral and physical condition

It has been represented to ns that many persons have misunderstood the meaning of the 9 of the Colonial Law, in relation to the stipulated income of $500 a year, strangely fancying that the law intended this should be the net income of an individual to entitle him to vote for members to serve in the Colonial Council, and many therefore, we are told, omitted to register their names on the lists sent round for the purpose of ascertaining the names of all persons qualified to vote under this clause. We therefore take leave to put such persons right on this point who labor under this delusion, and to assure them that the law has no reference whatever to what they do with their income ; it is enough if they only are in receipt of the amount in question yearly, produced either by their industry in trade, or derived from salary, or the investment of capital þÿ they are fully entitled to the privilege of j Colonial voting. If there be any persons then who have thus misconceived the law, we strongly advice them to call at the office of the Burgher Council and have their names placed on the list of voters without delay. We conceive it to be a privilege which no sensible man should lightly throw away.

FOR THE ST. CROIX AVIS. Till: COLONIAL LAW. Concluded þÿ see No. 88(5. From the Report the Committee of of the Landsthing it is perceived, that the honorable members proposed, that the following clause should be introduced into the Colonial Act, viz : that no tax should be imposed, altered or abolished except by law. What were the motives of the Rigsdag, tor not adopting this emendation of the original draft, we know not ; but it appears to us, that such a clause is of the last importance. Besides the powerful arguments adduced by the Committee in support of the measure, it is certain, that the greatest check the legislative power can hold on the executive is the right of granting or refusing the supplies. It may, however, be objected, that the functions of the Council are but consultative. 50 were those of the States General of the Mother Country ; we find, notwithstanding, in the ordinance of 28th May 1831, announcing the introduction of that institution, that no taxes or contributions could be levied prior to the opinion of the States General being elicited. Nor can it lie advanced as an adverse reason, that the Colonial Budget will in general be laid before the Council ere it will be passed. The right of taxation and that of expressing an opinion on the receipts end expenditures are two distinct eirn. instances. This will become evident, on referring to the fundamental law of the Mother Country. The 51 thereof contains a similar clause as that proposed by the Committee of the Landsthing; and yet the 52d % further
establishes the rule, that the Budget shall annually be brought before the Diet. That the sittings of the Colonial Assembly should be public, except when

deemed otherwise necessary, was like wise recommended by the Committee ot the Landsthing, but not adopted by the Diet. The public being present at the deliberations of the council would not only have caused members to keep up to their duty, but would have also prevented the discussions from becoming colloquial. The public would have then been able personally to judge the merits or demerits of their representatives, to weigh the arguments advanced in favor or against a measure, and to gain much from the debates of the collected wisdom of these Islands. They would have felt a greater interest for the institution. Notwithstanding the deficiencies in the Colonial Law, pointed out by us in the preceding remarks, we reiterate our thanks for the boon bestowed on us. We consider it a great acquisition. The law gives us legal means lor acquiring more extensive rights and priviliges. The electoral contest is about to com mence; its result will show whether we are worthy of more liberal institutions. Those legal means are of a pacific nature ; they are in harmony with the spirit of the age, the progress of ideas, and the interests of humanity. The exercise ol those rights excludes all agitation ; there may be individuals who will exult in our acting like men without þÿ political sense and þÿmoderation. Fellow citizens, let us avail ourselves ot' those legal means and recollect, that all of us individually and collectively, can only have one interest at heart þÿ the prosperity of these
Islands.

The captain of the brigantine Sally Evans had been committed to prison in Barbados on a charge of murder, having stabbed the steward of the vessel with a dagger, which caused his death. þÿ Several useful measures had passed the Legislature. Among others were two Bills, one for establishing a Savings' Bank, the other to authorize the introduction of Foreign machinery into the Island. A Bill to regulate the trade ol the Island, was under consideration. It was proposed to retain the Customs' Establishment on its present footing, with reference to the appointment and control of the officers remaining in the hands of the Board of Commissioners in England, but an amendment was moved and carried that the Board of Officers should be local, that is, that their ap-

Molasses, 5,679 puns., 175 liluls., and 168 barrels had been exported. We are indebted to the St. Lucia Palladium for the following from Guadaloupe. A project for the importation of 4000 labourers from the west coast of Africa, submitted in 1851 to the Legislative Assembly, by M. Boissard, has been referred anew to the Minister of Marine, the projector asking to be allowed 200 fr. a head for the immigrants, since 250 fr. a head are accorded to Capt, Blanc for Coolies. M. Boissard is supported by the Governors of Guadaloupe and Martinique, and by the Agricultural Society of the former island. In addition to certain stringent regulations against vagrancy and idleness recently established at Guadaloupe, the municipal authorities of Pointe-a-Pitre, with a view to the suppresssion of the many tumults and robberies complained of in that town, have introduced a series of regulations, embodying a number of þÿ porters, to be called þÿcommissionnaires, selected out of persons of well-established honesty, and wlio are made collectively answerable for the derelictions of the members individually; they are to bear a medal about their person ; and are to make good to the owners any articles that may be missing when entrusted to their care. Their principal business is to carry goods for the merchants, and the luggage of passengers. In case of fire, these commissionnaires are to present themselves under the orders of their superintendent to aid in the preservation of property. Their pay is fixed by the
Mayor, and certain penalties, not exceeding 15 fr. are to be paid by them, with forfeiture of their badge, for neglect of duty or other misconduct.
