The Orleans Property. þÿ The Paris cot respondent of llie Daily News writes, þÿ 1 understand that within the last few days the President has held a council of his most confidential advisers, Persignv, de Maupas, St. Arnaud, and one or two mote, to deliberate on the course to be taken in reference to the eventual decision of the Council of State in the matter of the Orleans property. If 1 am rightly informed, the following decision was agreed þÿto: If the judgment of the Council of State should be contrary to the pretensions of the Government, the affair will be allowed to take its course before the ordinary tribunals. If the decision of these tribunals should be in favour of the Orleans family, such a result will be equivalent to the judicial reversal of the decrees of Jan. 22. þÿI he Government will in that case take measures still more energetic. All the facts relative to fusion will be collected, as well as the refusals of oath and resignations, motived or not; all the intrigues of the Orleans family will be strung together. From these materials an elaborate police report will be composed, and this repoit, printed in the Moniteuii, will fie followed by a decree, ordering the general and absolute confiscation of all the property of the house of Orleans in France, instead of the partial confiscation already decreed on Jan. 22. The new decree would be executed immediately."

Destructive Inundation in Germany. þÿ The districts of Miihlhausen and Heiiigenstadt have been visited by a great calamity. The bursting of a water spout caused such a sudden rise in the waters of the Unstrut and

3 'J? 0 ft X & t a a other streams, that not only is the whole harvest of the present year destroyed, but the fields are covered with stones ani sand to such an extent that it will be impossible to bring them into cultivation for years to come. In a quart of an hour the Unstrul rose 18 feet above its usual level The loss of life is not yet known ; but it is feared it is considerable. In Dingelstadt 11 bodies bave been found, and 19 persons are missing. In the j district of Miihlhausen above 20 persons are reported as having been drowned, and between 20 and 30 more are suspected to have shared the same fate. The roads are everywhere destroyed, whole herds of cattle and sheep have been lost, and buildings have been so completely swept away that scarcely a j stone of them remains. The full extent of the loss of life and damage to property has not yet been ascertained. The Provisional Government in Erfurt has despatched commissioners to the locality to make the necessary communications. Appeals are .already made to the public for subscriptions in aid of the population of the district.

The late Accident to the Czar. þÿ A notice, containing some rather meagre details about the accident to the Emperor of þÿRussia s express train has at length found its way into the papers The train was composed of a locomotive, with tender, a baggage-waggon, and an empty post-office carriage; then came a carriage full of Cossacks and servants, another with Prussian officers, and last of all the carriage with the Emperor, Prince Charles of Prussia, and the imperial court dignitaries. After passing the confines into Poland, the train, running at the rate of thirtyfive miles an hour, began to swing violently, in consequence of the unevenness of the rails, the sleepers having in many places rotted and given wav. A short distance beyond Myslowitz the driver, Ward, felt a jeik and saw that the baggage- waggon immediately behind the tender was off the rails. He gave the signal to put the breaks hard on the hinder carriages, at the same time letting on full steam, whereby he hoped to force the waggon back to the rails. Rut the chain broke, and off went locomotive and tender at terrific speed. The empty post-office carriage upset, the carriage with the Cossacks and servants was very much damaged. The i carriage with Prussian officers also got off the rails, and was nearly upset, the vehicle with the emperor remained with one wheel on the rails. Some of the Cossacks and ser- ! vants, it is admitted, were considerably hurt, and the Prussian officers received light contusions. If this be really the whole extent of

damage, it is a most singular occurrence. But the number of railway engineers, inspectors, watchmen, and even directors, who will be dispatched Siberia for thus bring- to ing the þÿCzar l s ife into jeopardy will assuredly form an awful list.

Oh, the thirsty earth ! How she waits and wishes For the kind refreshing shower, Coming down in gushes ; How she opens her pores, How she spreads her bosom, Pleading for the withered grass. And the sealed-up blossom l

Long the keen east wind þÿO er her daily sweeping, Parched her breast, and killed Flying tilings and creeping. From the arid soil, Green shoots peeped and faded And all things round appeared Withered, worn, and jaded.

Now and then a cloud In the west appearing, Gave a short-lived hope That the vane was veering ; But soon back it flew To the eastern quarter. And the cry became more loud þÿ þÿ Water! give us water þÿ!

First it fell like dew ; Scarcely one perceived it ; But how joyfully the earth On her breast received it 1 Flower and grassy blade, And all living creatures, Hailed the boon as suited best With their different natures
Faster now it came, Faster yet þÿ down-pouring. Mid the grateful trees, Like a torrent roaring þÿ With a sweep and swirl, With a gust and eddy ; Sudden it grew calm þÿagain Falling soft, and steady.

Oh ! the gladsome sound Sets all nature singing : On þÿearth bosom s now Thick the grass is springing, Man will now have grain, Cattle juicy clover. Shout, ye valleys and ye lulls. For the drought is over !

The French þÿNavy. In the appendix to the budget of the minister of marine is given a list of all the ships of war, frigates, steamers, Ac., in the possession of the French government, with a statement of the present position of the ships building. From this return it appears that the total number of vessels of all kinds and sizes in the French war navy amounts to 334, of which 24 arc ships of the line, 38 frigates, 28 corvettes, 42 brigs of war, 6 cannonieres (brigs), 35 light vessels, and 35 transports, varying from 800 to 350 tons, 1 steam ship of war (960 horse-power), 20 steam frigates of from 650 to 4.50 horse-power, 29 steam corvettes, and 70 steam avisos, 4 ships of war on the mixed system (sails and steam), 1 frigate, 2 corvettes, and I aviso. Besides these there are 67 ships of different kinds on the stocks þÿ namely, 22 ships of war, 18 frigates, 2 corvettes, 3 brigs, 2 steam men-of-war, 2 steam frigates, 5 steam corvettes, and 3 steamers of smaller size. This is a very formidable navy, hut it is still more so when it is considered in what an extraordinary state of efficiency it is kept. There is hardly a ship in the French navy that inot fit for sea, and that is not in a posi tion to be sent on service within a few week.

New York Weekly Herald, June 5, 1852. Kossuth on the Destiny of the United States. Every attentive observer of the course of Kossuth, every one who regularly reads his speeches and compares them one with another, must be struck with the manner in which he shifts his ground continually, and changes and modifies his opinions. He has no stability of principle þÿ no fixed ideas upon any political subject. The Herald appears to furnish him with his principal ideas. We are happv at being enabled to enlighten the Magyar We have chastened and sobered him down considerably since his arrival on our shores As an example of this, we may refer to his speech at Syracuse, on Monday last, in which he borrows the leading idea we put forward in an article commenting on his great farewell speech at Faneuil Hall. It will be in ! the recollection of the reader that, in that speech, as indeed in all his previous speeches, he insisted upon the United States going back to Europe to mingle in the strife and diplo-

power on the þÿearth. We showed that this was contrary to the great law of humanity, by which, since the foundation of the world, the march of civilization, and conquest, and dominion þÿ the light of science and literature þÿ all moral, intellectual, and religious light þÿ proceeded from east to west, as steadily as the course of natural light in the same direction, or the current of electricity from pole to pole, and that it would be reversing this great law for the United States þÿ leading the van of the civilization and dominion of the world þÿ to make a retrograde movement eastward. We showed that the instincts of the nation and its destiny were westward, and that the reversal of this law would be like stroking the back of a cat the wrong way þÿ from the tail to the head, instead from the head to the tail. We also showed, in the same article, that instead of going eastward to assail Russia, we were now actually in the Pacific, performing the destined circle which is to gird the world, and would, never cease going West till we met the East; and then perhaps we might take the Russian bear behind, if we saw fit þÿ not that this country has any particular antipathy to Russia, but because it will overthrow every obstacle in its onward course due west. Kossuth, convinced of his error, has caught our idea, and no longer talks of the United States going to Europe to fight its battle against Europe, but points to the opposite direction as the place of conflict between Russia and America. He says

Russia desires to become the master of Asia, because there England has founded, in immediate neighborhood and in direct opposition to Russian interests a mighty seat of power for the Anglo Saxon, so mighty and so full of future, that should even Russia kill by isolation the home-power of the British Islands, or even conquer them, either immediately or by one of her few consulates, still her dominion over the world and even over Europe, would be but a short dream, so long as the Anglo Saxon race threatens her verv existence from Asia ; the more, because now you, the other (and mark well) republican branch of the Anglo Saxon stock, melted in one mighty nationality of freedom with the Celtic and with the German race, never forgetting the oppression of the ancient homes, | I tell you, are brought t the same place of

3 tr» a t x 3. immedute conflict of interests with Russia, by the extension of your territory to the Pacific ocean, whence you are now drawn by a thousand natural ties of activity, towards þÿAsia. Thus Kossuth has completely shifted his ground as far as the East is from the West. But he is again wrong in one point. He talks of an immediate conflict with Russia in Asia. There it no prospect of any such thing. We have other work to do first. England, not Russia, is our great commercial rival, and to her from this continent and its islands, is hut a work of time, and one that comes before any possible conflict with Russia I he policy of the United Slates is a regard for her own interests; and under the prompting of that principle, Cuba, Canada, and the British Provinces, must be annexed before we drive Russia from the territory which she occupies on this continent. That is a work so easy, that when we want to do it, only two or three ships are necessary. And as for a future conflict with Russia in Asia, it is time enough to take care of that when the macy of its nations, and thus make itself þÿ a day arrives. The United States will then be so strong that nothing can resist her onward march, and Russia will probably yield before it without striking a blow. The best proof that the policy of this country is not to operate in the direction of Europe, but westward, by degrees, even to Asia itself, is the fact that no political platform can be got up that proposes intervention in European affairs ; but it is easy to get up a plat-

form to annex Canada or Cuba, because these belong to this continent, and are objects as immediately within our grasp, when we want to take them, as were Texas, New Mexico, and California. We have no doubt that in a short time Kossuth will again modify his views, to make them square with those of ihe Herald. Every dauber writes the name of the individual whose likeness lie pretends to represent under his daubings, being convinced that the similitude would otherwise never occur to the most lively imagination. The truth of this proposition is striking in the production of a paperstainer, in the last number of the invaluable þÿ Sanct Thonue þÿTidende. It we, notwithstanding, stop to notice his rabid lucubrations, it is owing to the circumstance of his styling himself þÿ þÿVeritas, shows and to that of his insensate outpourings appearing in a paper, the motto ot which is þÿ Truth and þÿJustice. Veritas, aware of the gullability of the immaculate Editor of the Tidende, begins by paying him the compliment, that T. ()., fearing that bis production would not find room in the columns of the Tidende, had it inserted in the St. Croix Avis. The Editor in his simplicity gulped the bait, and hence the world is bewitched with the wonderful penmanship of Veritas in the Tidende. Veritas may, however, rest assured, that we do not envy him the felicity of obtaining a space in the Tidende for his production, which bids fairly to transform it into a þÿ LyingþÿPost. To vent his hypocondrical vapours on the bureaucracy, Veritas not only perverts the truth, and thus unblushingly profanes the holy name he has dared to assume, but asserts what he is certain is notoriously false. In qouting from our article he declares, that þÿ þÿ we (the Bureaucracy) mustered strong and formed a þÿphalanx <fcc. Now on re-

ferring to the article, it will be evident to every one but a Verit as, that we did not nor could not allude to the bureaucracy, when we said, that we mustered he is aware, strong. If Veritas was at the meeting, that the bureaucracy þÿ except one or two þÿ did not take any part in the proceedings. If Veritas was absent he has read the report of the Meeting in the Tidende. He has, therefore,

<0 Ui (0 A T 1 3 wilfully attempted to palm a gross falseon the public. And the miserable shift resisted to by him in adding the word bureaucracy to the sentence bears in the very face of it the most unqualified contradiction of his assertion. In his hurry to charge us with misrepresentation, Veritas has stamped the proceedings of the meeting with ridicule. He accuses us of having omitted the words þÿ þÿapproved, if which proves, says our modern þÿ þÿDemosthenes, that there was no obligation to be þÿincurred. Consequently all the electors were to be inveigled to declare themselves to be as stu pid as Veritas. The quotation of Veritas from a pretended English paper, we confess is truly applicable þÿ not to the voters of St. Thomas þÿ but to Veritas and his friend Simplicitas. Veritas will no doubt claim the merit of the quotation, and leave the stigma to the natural bashfulness of the Editor of the Tidende. St. Thomas, 8th July 1852. T. St. Thomas Times, .lull / 7, 1852. To the Editor of the St. Thomas '.rimes. Sill, þÿ Permit me through the medium ot your paper to convey to the people of St. Thomas, some information respecting Liberia, the 44 New þÿRepublic which is attracting the attention of nearly all civilized nations and affording an asylum of rest and comfort to the oppressed Sons of Africa, but of which 1 believe the inhabitants of your Island generally know but little. Liberia you are aware is situated on the western coast of Africa, between the parallels of 4r and 7 north latitude, and 8 and 12 west longitude. It was founded in the year 1821, by an association of benevolent men in the United States, who considering the unfavorable situation and degraded condition of the colored people among them assumed the denomination of, 44 The American Colonization þÿSociety. with a view of re moving ilw free colored people from beneath the oppressive influence of prejudice, to a place where they might he out of its reach. Accordingly they fixed upon Africa as the place, þÿ and no other could be more eligible than this, the land of their forefathers, where many now sit beneath their own vine and fig-tree (or palm tree), none daring to molest or make them þÿafraid. For 20 years Liberia continued under the fostering care of the Colonization Sociotv. In the year 1847, on the 20th day of July, it became independent, and is now recognized bv three of the þÿ great powers" of Europe, and we have every reason to hope that the others will soon follow their example. Yes,

Sir, Libet ia holds a position among the nations of the earth Her Government is purely republican þÿ the Chief Magistrate is elected every two years by the people þÿ the Legislature meets annually. The Senators and Representatives are voted for by the people, &e. &c. What is more, there is not a white man engaged in the control of lie r public aflairs. Her Officers of State. Preachers, Physicians, ktc., are all colored men of intelligence and sterling republicanism þÿ and. considering the meagre advantages they have had for the acquisition of knowledge, they might be said to be learned. The means of education are just now becoming general ; hitherto they have been few and limited. There are now several fine schools in Liberia two of them in Monrovia are under the auspices of the Presbyterian Hoard of Foreign Missions þÿ t he Alexander High School under the tuition of Reverend David A. Wilson. A M., þÿ which I attend as a student þÿ and the preparatory or English Department under 15. V. R. James, Esquire. These schools I believe to be the most efficient in Liberia. We expect soon to have a college, for which at the last session of the Legislature a piece of Land on the St Paul's was appropt iated. Agriculture isalso on the advance. The enterprising farmets on the banks of the St. Paul and St John Rivers are embarking largely in the cultivation of coflee, which will doubtless be a source of some wealth to our citizens; sugarcane isalso raised to some extent. Everything that is raised in the

West Indies can be raised fiere in great abundance with little trouble þÿ plantains, bananas, potatoes, cassadas. yams, &c. We have a variety of fruits. Such is the productiveness of the soil, that with a little labor on a small farm, a man with a family of three or four, may live very comfortably. Poultry and stock may be raised in any quantity. Here then is a home for the coloted man þÿ a home fraught with happiness, and the means ol comfort. We do not say that there is a prospect of accumulating a large amount of money, but a man can live comfortably. The country is new, and its resources as a consequence are yet limited. 44 The love of þÿliberty then should influence colored men to come. Every man that desires to come, should come with a view to assist in building up an asylum þÿ establishing a home, where in the enjoyment of liberty and happiness, his posterity might forever repose.

Liberia is also exerting a considerable influence on the heathen around. Many have adopted civilized habits, and rejoice in an opportunity of having their children taught to read. Some, under the influence of the gospel, have been brought to ,l sit at the feet of Jesus in their right þÿminds. The cruel and abominable slave-trade has been entirely abolished within the limits of Libeiia, which embrace more than 300 miles of coast. Africa has doubtless suffered much, but the darkness and gloom of heathenism are receding at the approach of the light of civilization. Superstition and cruelty are disappearing before the match of the þÿ free Sons of Liberia" ; and the strong-holds of Satan, standing for centuries, are bein'; demolished by the powerful þÿ hammer that "breaketh the rocks in þÿpieces þÿ In a word, Western Africa is under a recuperative influence, which will tell well on generations yet unborn. O yes, in spite of all the malice and opposition of the wicked one, " Ethiopia shall stretch out Iter hands unto þÿGon. þÿ White on the distant Hindoo shore þÿMessiah Cross s is reared, While Pagan votaries bow no more With Idol blood besmeared, While Palestine again doth hear The Gospel's joyful sound. While þÿIslam crescents s disappear From þÿCalvary holy s ground, Say, shall not þÿAfric fated s laud With news of grace be blest ? Say, shall not Ethiopia's band Enjoy the promised rest þÿ! Yours rcspectfull v, EDWARD ULYDEN. Alexander High School, Monrovia, Liberia, ) April, 1852. )

Louis Napoleon threatening tlie English Press. From the Daily News, Jane H). Impunity is said to beget insolence þÿ and that it does so we iind new proof in the last act of Louis Napoleon. Without his þÿuncle genius, s he has- many of that þÿuncle s failings; and amongst the rest inherits the First þÿConsul inability s to discover where it is wise to stop. Having overrun Italy and Germany, the uncle ventured upon Russia: havingfleccecl France of her liberties, the nephew ventures upon something very like insult to English freedom. The gagged press of France lies helpless at his feet þÿ and now he seeks to intimidate the free press of Fugland. On Tuesday the agent of the French police, who has under his special charge the newspapers of France, sent for the Paris correspondents of two or three of the London daily papers, that he might communicate to them the future intentions of l.ouisNapoleon towards theEnglish press, in performing this task, the agent, M. Latour Domoulin, is described as bringing the manners and language of cultivated lite to bear upon the work in hand, evidently in order that its real character might seem less abominable. Rut tyranny, however bland, is still tyranny, and in this case there was no room for mistake. In his interview with the correspondent ofthe Express, thefirstintimation M. Domoulin gave was, that what lie was about to state must he regarded as an official notice of the French Government. He then went on to say that the English newspapers had been outrageous towards the President, and added that in all fu-

ture cases when anything offensive appeared in the columns of an English newspaper, its representative in Paris would be made responsible for it, and he forthwith expelled from France ! Astonished by such a threat, our correspondent replied :

iV -Jk ® 'JS B I AT S 3 þÿ That if the French government made the Paris correspondent ot an English paper responsible for whatever appeared in that paper relative to France, it would act neither according to the principles of justice, law, nor international usage. It wits known that responsibility could only lie with the editor of the newspaper in England. A correspondent formed no part of what the French call the redaction of a paper. He was a private person, who sent confidential letters, the responsibility of whose publication he had nothing whatever to do with. The remedy ofthe FrenchPresident lay clairly against the newspaper, which he might either prosecute in the English courts of law, or lay a diplomatic complaint against with the English government, which would, in point of fact, come to the same thing; only in the latter case the French government would hold the English authorities responsible lor the prosecution ofthe paper. The French government had recently followed such a course in Belgium. When the Prince þÿPresident suncle became emperor, he was attacked with violence by a paper, and he took this means of redress, lie caused it criminal information to he filed against the editor of the newspaper, who wits defended by Sir James Mackintosh. The upshot of the affair was the condemnation ofthe newspaper to considerable damages. M. Latour Dumoulin answered that the French government could not accept the theory of irresponþÿsibility. Louis Napoleon will hold it Paris correspondent liable, he says, for what an

editor in England may say of his acts, although he knows perfectly well that a correspondent hits no more influence over the leading columns ofthe paper he writes for, than over the Royal Gazelle at St. Petersburg!!. Rut the editor is beyond the þÿPresident jurisdiction s þÿ the correspondent is in his power; and so upon the innocent lie threatens to wreak the vengeance impotent to reach those who offend him by telling truth. In the old barbarous days a similar despotism was often indulged. Many it successful tyrant has murdered, in cold blood, the wife and children of an opponent who was out of reach, and now one man is to he punished Paris because another is in troublesome in London. Was there ever a more unblushing stretch 'of power than to make it man responsible for that over which he has no control'/ Rut having, tor a time, succeeded in stopping free discussion in France, the hero of the coup if etat seeks to force the meshes of his tyranny across the English Channel. Ilis agent talks ot the dissemination of þÿ false þÿnews; hut it is not false news that offends, hut true. Is the story ofthe coup d'etat þÿ false þÿnews/ Is the tragedy of the unarmed Parisians shot down by thousands in the streets in Decemberþÿ is that þÿ false þÿnews/ Is the list of eminent and patriotic Frenchmen exiled from their country þÿ false þÿnews/ Are the groans of thousands transported without trial to Cayenne þÿ þÿnews? Are the refusals ofthe best generals and statesmen of France to take

the oath to Louis þÿNapoleon g s overnment þÿ are they þÿ false þÿnews/ Are the the decrees ordering the spoliation of the private property ofthe Orleans family þÿ false news? Yet these are the things that have made the free journals of this country couple Louis þÿNapoleon n s ame with those terms that make him anxious to expel English writers from France, and these are things let him remember which have become part of the sad story ofthe fine country he now holds in bondage. It no other news came from Paris for a century, here is a catalogue full enough of texts for volumes of written condemnation.

. j Rut does Louis Napoleon think it possible for him to expel every Englishman from France? Because until he does so he may rely upon it the Express and the other London daily papers will have intelligence of all that happens there. If our present correspondent were expelled to-morrow we have another ready on the second þÿ instant to iill his post. Let him expel a and a third will spr ingup. There are Frenchmen, too, as well as Englishmen ready for such emergencies. If the President carries on this system, as each writer is expelled he will find þÿ another and another still þÿsucceed. So long as this journal is faithful to that cause which it was founded to promote, and from which it has never swerved, so long will no threats and no fear of consequences prevent it from speaking what is known to he the truth. 3 UN ©»<£> JtX &T 18 THE tinies tlie momentous undersigned, þÿ of these Colonies and and lastin',' influence actuated by conviction may be a on principally the des- of of this Island, which the first Colonial Assembly will exercise, that Assembly most likely having to discuss Drafts of laws respecting Exercise of Trade, Mercantile and Mechanical, þÿ Relations of .Masters and Servants, of Planters and Laborers, þÿ Vagrancy, þÿ and in fact nearly all the relations that will more or less influence the well-being of the community and of the individual members of the same þÿ have thought it their duty to consider the means of best securing a free and effective exercise of the right of vote granted to the inhabitants by the Colonial Law. It is at once obvious, that no beneficial result can be obtained, if the qualifications of the individuals to be voted for are not discussed by the voters, and it is likewise obvious, that such discussion will be very unsatisfactory, if it be restricted to the trivate circle of each voter. The consequence of such an unsatisfactory discussion may be either that voters will vote at random, or from a caprice, or that they, will from diffidence or other motives less creditable stay away from the voting. Roth results we would consider very lamentable and derogatory to the dearest interests of the inhabitants, and at the same time an opprobrium on the voters. We have considered a trial-election by ballot the best means of obviating these evils. Such ballot, if generally attended to, will give voters an opportunity

of finding out the general feeling in the District in regard to such individuals, that may be proposed. When the result of the ballot is made known, we would consider it a matter of course, that only such individuals as have by the trial-voting obtained a reasonable numlier of votes should be voted for at the actual election. Thus canvassing for votes would reasonably be limited to such individuals that according to the trialvoting could be considered to have a chance, and the voters would avoid the disagreeableness to be called upon for votes by individuals whom they of themselves would not think of voting for, a consideration of some moment in a community, where a considerable part of the voters would be more or less dependent on employers or customers, relations that ouuiit not to INFLUENCE THE VOTING. We therefore invite voters residing in the jurisdictions of Christiansted and Frederiksted to assemble in the respective districts at a time and at places to be advertised, when the lists of voters are ready, in order to ballot for five members of the Colonial Council for Rasin and three for Westend, the numbers to be voted for in the respective districts. It is to be remarked, that voters from any district may be elected. A Committee of the undersigned will bo present to register the votes, the result of which will be made publicly known on the spot and in the St. Croix Avis. St. Croix, Christiansted :18th June 1852. To the Did. The undersigned inhabitants of the Island of St. Croix, who, on the 3rd July 1848, were slave-owners, have the honour of adressing the Danish Diet with a petition tending to secure its assistance in obtaining the compensation, they consider themselves entitled to in consequence of the emancipation of their slaves. After we in the distress, this event had reduced us to, and which to many amongst us involved the loss of all their property, had repeatedly addressed llis Majesty the King and the Ministry ot Finances, which was entrusted with the direction of the Colonies, with petitions for such compensation, without thereby attaining any result, the Ministry has at last laid before the last Diet the draft of a law, granting compensation to the former owners of slaves in these Colonies, but so late, that the Diet could not find time to proceed further in the matter than to a preliminary and cursory discussion. It is to be expected, that the draft will he made the subject of further deliberation in the impending Diet, and we must therefore not neglect as well to recommend our cause to the same, as also to point out the little satisfactory manner, in which the Ministry in the said draft has thought convenient to despatch our claim, w hich it, refusing to acknowledge it as a legal one. still at ihc same time admits to be founded on equity and justice. We cannot admit as valid the distinction, draw n by the Ministry and several members of the last Diet between the

right of property in slaves and that in other goods, so far as the conclusion is concerned which this distinction is to lead to, in regard to the compensation question. Tn this respect the distinction is void of all legal and practical foundation, and the restrictions in the exercise of the right of property, upon which one has based such a distinction, and which one very incorrectly styles restrictions of the right itself, can neither according to general legal notions, nor to analogies, derived from the limitations, to which the use of about all other kinds of property is subjected, nor to common reason, he of any effect when the question of indemnification for an abolished right of property is discussed. Any right of property is, regarding its exercise, limited by certain necessary and rational bounds, which of course do and must vary according to the object being either an inanimate and irrational one or a human creature. But, we repeat, this restriction affects merely the exercise of the right, not its essence and substance, O 7

The greater or less, the more general or more particular limitation of a right is a fact, which ceases to exist with the right itself, and which, as long as it existed, was one of the factors, that served to fix its value in commerce. Does the right cease, it ceases with the value, which was determined by the restriction, and the latter can not naturally, after having accomplished its a effect, which again to effect value, be called upon it previously had already served to fix. Thus this value is no other but the identical one, the object of property was invested with, at the time of the abolition of the right. It is easy to determine the same, the more so, as it can be traced in the valuation of slaves, fixed and revised by the Government and of Council for the purpose the Burgher regulating and moreover compulsory sales in effecting the prices obtained by self-liberation, the Royal Treasury itself lor the slaves, belonging or mortgaged to same, which were sold even up to a period, shortly preceding emancipation. It is but right here to remark, that the cipated in all such transactions, Royal Treasury has at all times the parti- object of which was purchasing, selling, mortgaging slaves, that it yet is in possession of bonds, stipulating expressly the right of mortgage not only in landed properties with their inventory ol slaves, but even in the persons ol slaves, that

are unconnected w ith any such property, and that the said Treasury now most rigorously calls upon with the capital together its debtors to pay 0 per cent interest, due for purchased slaves, refusing even to comply with the otten-repeated petition, to grant delay for further payments until after a final settlement ol the emancipation question. The Ministry, in refusing to acknowledge our legal claim to compensation, has thrown out this assertion without any proof. And such proof cannot be adduced. It may be tempting, when one by a public position the make a proposition, is necessitated to unpopularity ot which one is aware ot, to proclaim, that the weaker part, that would be benefited by the same, has and to get anything, in fact no legal claim thus to exhibit þÿone s feeling and equity justice, for, what ot one under such a supposition agrees to give one accords trom mere generosity and at the same time gains the right ot arbitrarily fixing the amount ol the gilt. But order in to maintain such a position, one must prove it, so, what is the same, prove, that there did not exist any right of property over slaves, and this would he nothing else, but to prove what is in itself contradictory. Our whole legislature, as far as it regards the Colonies, acknowledges slaves as legal property, the whole social order in the Colonies is based upon slavery as a matter ot right, particular existing tie jure and de facto, the and exer- restrictions, which the cise of the right of property over slaves

must be subject to, do not, as we above have proved, affect the right itself. i\ow it is a principle, acknowledged and established in the whole Danish just as well as in the legislature of all other civilized nations, that the right of property is sacred and inviolable, and that it cannot be abolished but where the common weal required it, and even then only with full compensation. In further corroboration of this truth we can not only adduce t he contents ot a Placard, dated 31st July 1755, but with special reference to the West Indies the law ot 30th April 1755, $34, according to which the owner is to be compensated for the slave, sentenced to death, the law ot 1st May 1840, resolving, that the owners of

m nmn< r ..vwi slaves should be obliged to give up their right of property for full compensation. In regard to an argument, used by the Mother Country against our claim to compensation, 1847 of 28th Julv viz: that the Rescript had fixed a term for the expiration of slavery, we have simply to observe, that the said Rescript passed over the compensation-question anti left it undivided and that already in the first meeting of the commission, appointed for the purpose of making propositions for carrying into effect the contents of the Rescript, the members urged the claim of compensation, to be enforced together with the emancipation. It would however in itself be useless to adduce this Rescript, which was partly looked upon as little suitable, partly remained a dead letter and which, if really put into execution, would have created a miserable and intolerable condition in the Colonies. It has amongst other arguments been maintained, and, even so far as we have been able to learn, from this very Island, that the slave owners had suffered no loss by emancipation, and therefore had no claim to compensation from the same source has been urged, that slavery could not exist any longer, because it had outlived itself, and that emancipation was only formal corroboration of this result. Common sense, will, we trust, dispense us from refuting all the garbled statements and arguments, which emanate from people, that are devoid either of good will, or the capacity of judging of these matters, in an

impartial and rational manner. If it thus must he acknowledged, that we had a legal right of property in our slaves, that this right was annulled against our will and through no fault of ours and that we thereby have sustained severe losses, it is palpable, that we are entitled to full compensation from the State. But full compensation is very different from the one offered by the Ministry. Full compensation is the market price of the slave at the time of emancipation. If one, in order to urge practical difficulty unfair which would be and a further delay, to us, will fix a certain average price for each slave, we can have no objection. But instead of that we are offered $40 in bonds, which we would not even realize, which are to be cancelled in the course of 13 years and only bear 4 per cent interest, to begin from the fourth anniversary Such the destruction of our property. of a bond would, as the legal percentage here is 6 per cent, only be realized at a loss of at least 20 per cent, is that we instead of $40 would in reality only receive $32 for a slave, and besides lose 4 þÿyears interest or 24 per cent of the capital. Such a settlement, were it even a mere claim of justice and equity, appears to us neither just nor fair. The financial position of the Mother Country herself has been urged as an impediment, preventing her from to ing us a compensation adequate grant- the full value of our slaves. That she in justice and equity can demand of us, that we should allow some influence on

the amount of compensation and the form of disbursement to this incontrovertible fact we joyfully concede, though this argument appears not to have exercised any influence on the amount of indemnification fixed for damages of war or the equalization of privileged and unprivileged lands. But, in allowing such a concession to be made, we must still militate against the unfairness of the ministerial proposition, and we do hereby with unlimited confidence recommend our just cause to the chosen representatives of the Danish nation and thus we seek our right, where right was never denied.

Charles C. Rafn's work, Antiquitates American®, published by the Society in 1837, was intended to establish and elucidate the discovery of America by the

Scandinavians in the tenth century. Tiie result of the published historical sources, and of þÿRain researches s which are founded upon them, was, that the Scandinavians in the loth century discovered, and in the lltli and immediately following centuries, repeatedly visited, the lands lying on or near the Eastern coasts ot North America, that is, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, and New England, and of the latter particularly Massachusetts and Rhode Island. This result can now he regarded as recognised by the inquirers who have made this matter a subject of independent study. Among European scholars, Alexander Humboldt has lately in his Cosmos (vol. 11, p. 269-272 of the Germ, ed.) fully adopted this historical fact. A concise memoir upon the discovery of America in the tenth century by Rafn lias been inserted in English in the beginning of tiie Antiquitates American®, from which it was copied into the Journal of the Royal Geographical Society of of Ixmdon, vol. VIII ; it was again printed in French in tiie Society's Mi-moires 1836-1839, p. 27-55. The nautical and geographical evidences contained in the old writings, upon which the investigations are based, are, without doubt, fully sullicent to sustain the results which have been drawn from them. But in addition to these we have an astronomical testimony in the statement concerning tiie length of the shortest day. This was treated also in the main work, but it seemed capable of being elucidated with yet greater clearness.

The safety and importance of this testimony will be perceived from the brief treatise which the author lias inserted in tiie þÿ Mi-moires des Antiquaires du þÿNord, 1810-1844, p. 128 et seq. and in the þÿ Antiquites Amcþÿricaines published in 1845, p. 15-16. Rightly apprehended and understood, tins evidence is as sale and reliable as the nautical and geographical proofs, with which, in its result, it perfectly accords. Discredit has been given to single points, which are of subordinate importance, and which, in any case, can have no hearing upon tiie main result which is founded alone upon the old writings and their correct interpretation. in this manner, Blackwell, in Ids edition of Mallet's Northern Antiquities, London 1847, while lie recognises the main result as wholly reliable, has nevertheless cast doubt on some of the details. Meanwhile he lias shown us in another place, the point of view from which lie wishes to be regarded, by unreservedly declaring that lie considers it questionable whether the Danish King, Ragnar Lodbrok, ever existed ! Traditional history demands a separate regard, but Agamemnon lias his place in history, and just as certainly Ragnar Lodbrok. (To be continued.)

The Pic Shops of London. Some time since, so runs ihe current narrative, the owner of a thriving muiton-pie concern, which, after much difficulty, lie had succeeded in establishing with borrowed capital, died before he had well extricated himself from the responsibilities of debt. The widow carried on the business after his decease, and throve so well, that a speculating baker on the opposite side of the way made her the offer of his hand. The lady refused, and the enraged suitor, determined on revenge, immediately converted his baking into an opposition pie-shop ; and acting on the

principle universal among London bakers, of doing business for the first month or two at a loss, made his pies twice as big as he could honestly afford to make them. The consequence was that the widow lost her custom, and was hastening fast to ruin, when a friend of her late husband, who was also a small creditor, paid her a visit. She detailed her grievance to him, and lamented her lost trade and fearful prospects. þÿ Ho, ho!" said her friend, þÿ that þÿ ere s the move, is it? Never you mind, my dear. If I þÿdon git t your trade again, there aint no snakes, matk þÿme þÿthat s all þÿI So saying, he took his leave. About eight o'clock the sameevening, when the þÿbaker s new pie-shop was crammed to overflowing, and the principal was below superintending the production of a new batch, in walks the þÿwidow friend s in the costume of a kennel-raker, and elbowing his way to the counter dabs down upon it a brace of huge dead cats, vociferating at the same time to the astonished damsel in attendance, þÿ Tell your master, my dear, as how them two makes six-and-thirty this week, and say þÿI ll bring t'other four to-morrer arternoon þÿ! With that he swaggered out and went his way. So powerful was the prejudice against cat-mutton among the population of that neighborhood, that the shop was clear in an instant, and the floor was seen covered with hastily-abandoned specimens of every variety of segments of a circle. The spirit-shop at the corner of the street experienced an unusually large demand for þÿ goes of brandy,

and interjeciional ejaculations not purely gramrttatical were not metely audible, but visible, too, in the district. It is averred that the ingenious expedient of the widow's friend, founded as it was upon a profound knowledge of human prejudices, had the desired effect of restoring þÿ the balance of trade." The widow recovered her commerce ; the resentful baker was done as brown as if he had been shut up in his own oven ; and the friend who brought about this measure of justice received the hand of the lady as a reward for his interference. þÿ þÿHarper Magazine. s

Iron Paper. þÿ At the Ptussian Industrial Exhibition, Count Renard, a large proprietor of ironworks, exhibits sheet-iron of such a degree of tenuity that the leaves can be used for paper. Of the finest sort the machinery rolls 7,040 square feet, of what may be called leaf-iron, from a cwt. of metal. A bookbinder of Breslau has made an album of nothing else, the pages of which turn as flexibly as the finest fabric of linen rags. As yet no extensive application for this form of the metal has been found, but the manager says the material must precede the use for it. Perhaps books may hereafter be printed for the tropics on these metallic leaves, and defy the destructive power of ants of any colour or strength of forceps. We have only to invent a white ink, and the thing is done.

3 'JK 1 ATI 8k THE undersigned, actuated the momentous and þÿ lasting influence by a conviction of on the destinies of these Colonies and may be principally of tills Island, which the first Colonial Assembly will exercise, that Assembly most likely having to discuss Drafts of Laws respecting Exercise of Trade, Mercantile and Mechanical, þÿ Relations of Masters and Servants, of Planters and Laborers, þÿ Vagrancy, þÿ and in fact nearly all the relations that will more or less influence the well-being of the community and of the individual members of the same þÿ have thought it their duty to consider the means of best securing a free and effective exercise of the right of vote granted to the inhabitants by the Colonial Law. It is at once obvious, that no beneficial result can be obtained, if the qualifications of the individuals to be voted for are not discussed by the voters, and it is likewise obvious, that such discussion will be very unsatisfactory, if it be kf.stkicted to the private circle of each voter. The consequence of such an unsatisfactory discussion may be either that voters will vote at random, or from a caprice, or that they, will from diffidence or other motives less creditable stay away from the voting. Both results we would consider very lamentable and derogatory to the dearest interests of the inhabitants, and at the same time an opprobrium on the voters. We have considered a trial-election by ballot the best means of obviating these evils. Such ballot, if generally attended to, will give voters an opportunity

of finding out the general feeling in the District in regard to such individuals, that may be proposed. When the result of the ballot is made known, we would consider it a matter of course, that only such individuals as have by the trial-voting obtained a reasonable number of votes should be voted for at the actual election. Thus canvassing for votes would reasonably be limited to such individuals that according to the trialvoting could be considered to have a chance, and the voters would avoid the disagreeableness to be called upon for votes by individuals whom they of themselves would not think of voting for, a consideration of some moment in a community, where a considerable part of the voters would be more or less dependent on employers or customers, relations that ought not to INFLUENCE THE VOTING. We therefore invite voters residing in the jurisdictions of Christiansted and f'rederiksted to assemble in the respective districts at a time and at places to be advertised, when the lists of voters are ready, in order to ballot for five members of the Colonial Council for Basin and three for Westend, the numbers to be voted for in the respective districts. It is to be remarked, that voters from any district may be elected. A Committee of the undersigned will be present to register the votes, the result of which will be made publicly known on the spot and in the St. Croix Avis. St. Croix, Christiansted 28th June 1852. II K A F T of an Ordinance lo prevent Vagrancy in the Dunish West unfa J'ossessnms. I 1. l'ersons who are not known lo possess property, nor to have any fixed livelihood, nor any situation in life, which guarantees, that they derive their sustenance without detriment to the public, shall be called before the Police Magistrate to give an account of the manner in which they support themselves. 2. If the Individual's explanation itself or the ensuing investigation proves unsatisfactory, the Police Magistrate is to give him and in his ptesence enter in the protocol admonition to seek lawful maintenance, allowing him a certain time within which tie is to appear and prove that the admonition has been obeyed, in default of which he will he punished as a Vagrant. The Police Magistrate is authorized to dictate to the Individual, the observance of such rules, by which the Police are enabled to control, that the admonition given is attended to, in such a manner that the end in view of the same is actually attained; in case the individual be considered fit to take fixed service as house-servant, field-laborer, seaman, apprentice, or the like, the Police-Magisirate is likewise authorized to give him the necessary injunctions to this effect, in so far as he can obtain the same ; otherwise the Police-Magistrate is to assign him such service. Should the Individual in quesiion neglect the injunction in this tespect. he shall be punished as a Vagrant. 3. More particularly in case3 of public in-

vestigations respecting transgressions of th« Laws, as well as in Police-Cases relative to Encroachments upon property, Fights or Brawls, ns well as such regarding the relation between employers and laborers, masters and servants, the Police-Magistrate shall avail himself of the opportunity of demanding elucidations respecting the abode and livelihood of those persons, who may be implicated and of whom no sufficient knowledge is at hand, in order that it might he decided, in how far the rules laid down in the 1st and 2d $ of this

ordinance are applicable to them. If in cases of judicial investigation, that is not carried on by the Police-Magistrate, circumstances appear, that lead to suppose, that an individual has no lawful support, the respective Functionary shall thereof give notice in writing to the Police-Magistrate. 4. The following individuals shall likewise, without having received any admonition, be deemed Vagrants : 1) Persons who for a longer time than 14 days have illegally left their service, or their situation as fixed laborers in the country, and who on demand either cannot or will not acknowledge, where they in the mean time have been, or by what means they have been supporting themselves. 2) Persons without occupation who have tiad no fixed dwelling for a fortnight, and who cannot prove during that period to have gained their sustenance in a lawful manner. Abode on any landed property without the express consent of the proprietor or manager is not to be considered as a fixed dwelling in said respect. 5. Persons without occupation, who have been released after having undergone their punishment of imprisonment or public-work, are then in accordance with the 2nd to be enjoined to seek lawful support : þÿ and all such persons who have been sentenced to public work for a longer period than 0 months on account of Vagrancy, theft or other encroachments upon property shall moreover, be under the strictest control of the Police. | 6. Parents belonging to the country-population. have no right to commit their children

to the care of other persons in the towns, unless the persons by the Police-Magistrute are considered to possess such means, that the maintenance and education of such children in time to come can be secured, þÿ after which the necessary obligation in said respect, especially as regards the schooling of the child, is to be entered into by the foster-parents in the presence of the Poltce- Magistrate. Should children and persons under 18 years of age not be properly attended to by their parents or by those in lieu of parents, or these allow them to wander about in idleness, after their having arrived at that age, in wfiich they according to the circumstance, and condition of the parents might be placed to some steady occupation, the Police- Magistrate shall enjoin the individual in question within a certain lime to attend to his duties in said respect ; and should this injunction not be obeyed, the Police-Magistrate shall assign the minor proper occupation, in accordance with the Common l.aw B. 3. Ch. 18 7. Respecting children who have no parents nor any one in lieu of such in the Danish Wcstindia Possessions, the needful is to be attended to and ordered by the Police Magistrate ; which acts of his shall be laid before the higher authorities for approval. 7. Every owner of a house or of landed property is bound to render the Police Magis trate such elucidations as may be demanded in regard to persons residing on their property : and report shall within 48 hours be made

to the Police of all removals, without respect to the age of the individual. The punishment for Vagrancy for such 8< . persons who have not formerly been found guilty thereof, shall be imprisoned on Bread and Water from 48 to 4 times 48 hours with the respite ordained bv law. It shall be optional with the judge, according to circumstances, to apply imprisonment with hard labor instead of imprisonment on Bread and Water, thus: that in lieu of each 48 hours of the foTiner punishment imprisonment with hard lab« for 12 days shall be awarded.

When any person, having once been convicted of Vagrancy, is again found guilty of such, the punishment therefore shall according to circumstances be imprisonment on Bread and Water from 5 to 10 limes 48 hours, and in case of further repetiiion 10 to 15 tunes 48 hours or imprisonment with hard labor in proportion. If the Individual be detected anew in the same misconduct, the punishment shall be imprisonment with hard labor from 6 to 12 months, and for each repetition thereof, the said punishment shall be further extended, however in no case hevond 2 years. 10 Children and other individuals under 18 years of age, who of their own accord leave the situation or occupation, to which lliev have been bound by their parents or other persons thereto authorised, shall be kept to the observance of iheir duties by proper chas tisement, and if ihe individual be of an age be tween 15 and 18 years, then, if required, punishment according to the 1st of tire Ordinance <>! 23d Mav 1840 relative to punishment on Bread and VVater, shall be awarded

Persons, who cannot be considered as Vagrants, but who are discovered to have taken abode during the night in yards, galleries, sheds, carriage-houses or such other places, where they are not entitled to tie, shall iherefore be subject to a fine or to imprisonment for some davs, provided their conduct Irom other reasons does not make them liable to severer punishment. 12. Owners or occupiers of houses, negleciing to make the report ordered in 7. respecting the removal of persons, shall be subject to a fine from 50 Cents to 5 dollars for each case Persons wilfully harbouring Vagrants or any person purposely returning incorrect re ports or entering into fictitious agreements in order to conceal transgressions or elusions of this ordinance or ofoiher existing regulations respecting cases relative to woik or to service, shall be punished by a fine from 1 to 100 dollars. In cases of repetiiion the punishment mav be doubled. 13. All cases in which any person is prosecuted for transgressions of this ordinance shall be carried on before and decided by the Police Courts. 14 This ordinance shall be enforced from the and from the same date ail prior regulations regarding Vagrancy in the danish westindia possessions are repealed.

To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Deae slr, In consequence of the meetings held on the 7th Instant in Christiansted and Frederiksted for the purpose of ascertaining by trial-voting the names of such as might probably tie elected as members for the Colonial Assembly which is about being formed, I feel induced through the medium of your paper to address a few questions, remarks and suggestions to those qualified as voters. Let me then ask these Gentlemen : Has the proposed object of these meetings, as stated " To prevent the employed from being biased by their in the Circular invitation by which they were called, employers and others" been obtained ? Certainly not, on the contrary there is now more scope given for canvassing and biasing the votes of individuals. We were told in West End by the Chairman of the meeting that the votes, given in, were not binding on the voter unless he himself considered them so. What then has been effected by that meeting ? Nothing else, as far as I can see, but the gratification of idle or intentional and hidden curiosity. One good however results from such proceedings. An eligible opportunity is now offered to others as well as to myself of expressing our sentiments on this subject, which it is to be hoped will be done for the furtherance of the public good. In this spirit then, now that the names of the nroliable members are known, I would further ask : YVhat is the purpose of a Diet and of a Colonial Assembly ? Of course, will be answered, to represent

the people and their rights, redress grievances and to projKjsc and make amendments where and when neeassary as far as lies in their power. What power will the Colonial Assembly have ? Very Jittle indeed, in fact it appears to me that it will be nothing more than a mere voice. Why then weaken our position, as there is every reason to apprehend will be done, if the actual election shew the same votes, which have appeared at the trial votings. Why return men as Representatives of the people who are in the employ and the interest of the Colony in opposition to the view of i pay of Government ? Can tbey faithfully represent

the Government, without breaking faith witli that Government which has every right to expect that her Salaried Servants are to carry out on all occasions her views and measures ? In other words, can they so far get over the first law of nature Sell Preservation" " as to run tbo risk of opposing, as Colonial Representatives, when necessary, tire views of that Government on which they are dependant for their Situations, Influence and Support ? These Gentlemen are, though ablo men, but men and we must not look for more from them, than what we may reasonably expect from men in such positions, particularly when others in the Island not similarly situated, are just as well qualified. Before concluding I beg leave to assure the Government-officers, alluded to, that I am not actuated by personal motives in these remarks, hut solely by a wish to state matters in their fair light, that the Colony may have as far as is consistent with the nature ami powers of the Colonial-Assembly, independant and effective representatives. The Council of State of the Canton of Vaud decided recently, it is said, at the request of the French Government, on applying to M. Thiers, who was within the last few days at Vevey, in that canton, the Federal decree relative to confining French refugees to some appointed place in the interior of the country. There was only one vote against this decision, and the Prefect, M. Bachelard, was charged to transmit the order. M. Th iers had hired a house at Vevey for the whole summer; and his family, which had gone there to meet him, had expected to remain in tranquility for the season. When the order was communicated to him he refused to accept the internement or location assigned him, and left Switzerland in preference to proceeding to Piedmont. It is said he will pass the autumn in Italy. Much indignation, both in France and Switzerland, has been caused by the proceeding, particularly as it is remembered that Louts Napoleon himself was once the subject of a request somewhat similar from the Government of Louis Philippe to that of Switzerland, and that the latter refused to yield to Louis Philippe on the point. on Various were afloat in Paris the subject. The rumours following, taken from the correspondence of a residing contemporary, has an air of probability: þÿ It appears that theresolution of the French Government, with respect to the illustrious historian, was rather sudden. While M. Thiers was in Italy, the instructions given to the agents of the French Government in that coun-

try were to the effect that, so far from giving him the least annoyance, or throwing obstacles in his way, they were to treat him, if they should fall in with him, with the greatest respect. But it appears that the visit of M. Thiers to Switzerland, coinciding as it did with that of the Duchess of Orleans to the same country, gave umbrage to the jealous mind of Louis Napoleon, lie could not be persuaded that the simultaneous visits of these two personages to the Helvetic Republic were accidental; and though he did not precisely discover what evil could come of the affair, even if it were a rendezvous, he determined to give a new reading to an old adage, and consider on trie ignotum pro compirutione. It appears that a letter written by M. Thiers, from Turin, to a friend in Paris, has been for some days past in circulation, and has, perhaps had some influence on his fate. In this letter M. Thiers pays a high compliment to the young King of Sardinia, and to the free institutions now established in that country, and expresses a hope that the day may come when France may have similar institutions, with as wise a Cabinet as that presided over by M. d'Azeglio to carry them on.

Los oi the " Duchess of Kent" Steamer. A collision of a most frightful character occurred on Thursday afternoon, last week, in the river Thames, off' Norlhfleet Point, by which the Duciiess of Kent, Margate and Ramsgale steamer, was run down by the Ravensboukne, bound to Antwerp with nearly 200 passengers and full cargo. It appears that the Ravensbourne was steaming down the river with full tide in her favour immediately in the wake of and just on the starboard side of the Meteor Gravesend steam boat. She arrived nearly opposite Norlhfleet Point about two o'clock On nearing the Point, the Duchess of Kent, Margate steamer, was seen coming up the river against tide and hugging the southern shore þÿ the tide running very strongly. The Kavensboukne was about three parts over the river on the Kent shore, and as she neared the Duciiess of Kent, the latter crossed, apparently with the object of passing between the Ravensbourne and the Meteor ; when, in an instant, consequent on the heavy way on the Ravensbourne, before the Duchess of Kent could cross her, she ran into her about twenty feet from the figure-head, or just before the windlass, on the starboard bow. The crash wns frightful ; the Duchess of Kent immediately began to fill, and to commence sinking, bows foremost. The scene among the passengers, a large number of whom were ladies with children, was truly frightful. The captain of the Ravensbourne finding that the Duchess of Kent was rapidly sinking, backed, when

the passengers rushed, in their fright, to the still sinking part of the ship. At this moment the Meteor arrived alongside, and the passengers and crew on deck were literally dragged on to her and the Ravensbourne, with one exception. This was a gentleman named Hale, a brewer, of Broadstairs, Isle of Thanet, who, being infirm, was unable to be reached. In the meantime the vessel sank, bows first, almost perpendicularly, the keel being lifted as she sank twenty or thirty feet out of the water. The captain of the Duchess of Kent, it is only due to him to state was, with the exception of Mr. Hale, the last to leave his ill-fated vessel. Mr. Hale, .though unable to assist himself from infirmity while on board the vessel, most extraordinary to relate, the moment he reached the water, struck out and kept himself afloat until rescued by one of the boats lowered from the Meteor. From the moment of the collision to the time the Duchessof KENTcntircly sank beneaththe surface of the water, was little more than eight or nine minutes ; and, but for the prompt assistance rendered by the crew of the Star packet Meteor, a great loss of life must have occurred. þÿ Ibid.

To <D A T I From the New York Herald. Tlic Art of Photography þÿ Its wonderful progress. Daguerreotyping has attained it degree of importance and perfection in this country, and especially in this city, that places it high among those arts that combine the useful with the beautiful ; and it is now established as a permanent business, in which a very large sunt of money is invested and a very large number of artists employed. The number of establishments in this city is about one hundred, and the average number of pictures taken amounts to about one thousand daily. The amount of capital embarked in the various departments of the art, throughout the United States, is estimated at four millions of dollars. The number of persons employed in manufacturing materials for the pictures, and in other ways connected with the business, in this country, is about 25,000. This may appear incredible to those unacquainted with the progress and extent of the art ; but our information is from the most authentic sources, and may be relied on as accurate. To trace the progress of this art from its first dawn to its present high position is both curious and instructive. The pictures produced by photography are generally called daguerreotypes, from the Frenchman Daguerre, who is supposed by many to be the inventor of the art, but who only reduced its principles þÿ which were discovered before þÿ to such a state of practical perfection as placed the art upon a permanent and useful basis. Others had known the science and theory of the si rt , and some had

made practical proficiency in copying landscapes and portraits by the action of light; but Daguerre was the first great master of the art, and so far excelled all others that the art itself was called by his name. It is also called photography þÿ which means engravings produced bylight ; and the term photogenic þÿ created or born of light þÿ has been also applied to the art; while Daguerre himself called it þÿheliography rthe art of making drawings by the sun. All these terms are expressive of the same idea þÿ light. The art combines the science of light and chemistry, and its two great principles were discovered two or three hundred years ago. One of these principles was discovered two centuries ago by Porta, a Neapolitan, who found that if light were admitted through a small circular aperture into a dark room, all the objects outside, from which rays were reflected through this aperture, would be painted on the opposite wall, just as all the objects reflecting rays of light to the eye are painted on the retina. He to found by the application of a lens the aper- that ture þÿ densing increasing, þÿ the light centralizing, and con- the images became wonderfully distinct. Porta applied this discovery to drawing, in order that persons unacquainted with that art might trace the object as painted upon a white card placed within the focus of the glass in a dark chamber. Here is the first idea of the instrument of Daguerre. This is the rude camera obscura, which litis since become so powerful by improve-

ments in the manufacture of lenses. The great desideratum was to secure the image thus impressed, and make it indelible, for it was as evanescent as an image in a mirror, only remaining as long as the object was before it. Niepce and Daguerre succeeded in fixing it by the application of another principle, discovered more than three hundred years ago. That principle is that the rays of the sun, under given conditions, will leave a black mark upon certain substances.

þÿ The origin of the discovery is curious, and bears a remarkable analogy to the discovery of Christopher Columbus. þÿ The enthusiast of Genoa set out with the idea that he could reach the East Indies by the west, and he found, not the East Indies, but what was far better þÿ America. The alchemists, in the middle ages, in their fruitless search for the elixir vita, and the transmuting stone, laid the foundation of the valuable science of chemistry. Among other things they succeeded in uniting silver with a marine salt, and produced a combination called " lune," or "argent come." In the work of Fabricius on metals, published in 150(5, this substance is noticed. It had the color and transparency of horn, but the fusibility and softness of wax. If exposed to the light, it changed to violet, and by the continued action ot light it became nearly black. This was lunar caustic, or, as it is now called, salts of silver, chloride of silver, or nitrate of silver. Cover a sheet of paper with a coating of this substance, and throw, by means of a lens, the form of some object upon the paper, and the parts covered by the figure will change to a dark color, while the rest of the paper will remain white. I'lace an engraving, done upon semi-transparent paper, upon the paper coated with chloride of silver, and expose both to the sun's rays, with the engraving uppermost, and that part of the prepared paper covered by the outline of the engraving will remain white, in consequence of the interception of the

rays, while all the rest, being accessible to the light, will be turned black. This is called the negative proof, because the impression on it will be white ; but byplacing this proof over the sensitive paper, and again subjecting both to the action of light, a positive proof is produced, the object being now dark, and the rest of the paper white. The alchemists were too busy in the pursuit of the philosopher's stone, and other visionary objects, to turn this important discovery to practical account, and it was reserved for modern science to bring it to the perfection of one of the finest and most exquisite of arts. A Frenchman many years ago succeeded in obtaining black profile portraits ; but his secret died with him. Wedgwood, an Englishman, the celebrated improver of the manufacture of porcelain, was the next to challenge public attention in connection with this art. He was desirous of obtaining, on paper coated with nitrate of silver, representations ot church windows, and of engravings, for his pottery ; but he failed, the images being too laint. His paper appeared in the journal of the Royal institution, in 1802. Sir 11. Davy also made experiments, but did not appear to be more successful. Neither could prevent the borders of their drawings from becoming black, nor could their pictures be examined in broad daylight, for as soon as exposed to the sun's ray's, the whole of the paper began to assume one uniform dark tinge. After these imperfect results, nothing was attempted, or at all

events attained, until Niepce and Daguerre, by their researches and labors, removed every obstacle, and established the art upon a lasting foundation, leaving the superstructure to be improved, beautified, and adorned, by future artists. To be continued.
