Each of these divisions elects a Speaker of its own body, and then proceeds to scrutinize the letters of election of the respective Members, so, that the one division scrutinizes the letters of election of the other, and vice versa. 3. As soon as this scrutiny has taken place the Assembly again meet together. Those Members whose right to sit in the Assembly has been found established, and whose letters of election by the respective Speakers, consequently have been delivered to the senior Chairman who proclaims their names that they may be acknowledged as entitled to seats and votes in the Assembly, must then when called on by the senior Chair-

man, proceed to take the oath required, by signing the Formula prescribed by (he King, and which previously will have been distributed for this purpose. In case objections have been made against the validity of any one's election, the respective Speaker must explain the matter to the Assembly, and after the discussion on this head is ended, the senior Chairman puts the ques-

tion to the vote, among those who are acknowledged as Members ot the Assembly. If more than half the number of votes declare the election void, it is annulled, otherwise it remains in lull force. Such a decision renders all future objections futile, and those whose letters of election are thus acknowledged must proceed to take the Oath as prescribed. The Formulas so signed are then to be received by the Secretary for sale keeping. 4 The Assembly then proceed to appoint their officers, viz; a Chairman, a Vice-Chairman, and a Secretary, (Col. Law 25). No one can without the consent of the Assembly decline the appointment. 5. The choice of a Chairman takes place by written votes, thus: each Member entitled to vote, writes on a slip of paper the name of the person he wishes chosen ; the Secretary then collects the votes and hand them over to the senior Chairman, who opens them and calls the names, which must then be noted by the Secretary on an alphabetical list of all the names of the Members, given him for this purpose, and which in case of doubt can be compared with the votes so deposited, in order to rectify possible mistakes. In the choice of a Chairman more than half the votes are required and if this be not obtained on the first voting, a new free election must take place. If the requisite majority of votes be not now obtained, the suffrages are to be limited to the two Members who obtained most votes on the second trial. If several have obtained an equal number of votes, age

decides the matter. As soon as the Chairman is chosen he causes, in a like manner, the election of a Vice-Chairman, and a Secretary. G. The Chairman directs the discussions in the Assembly and sees that good order be observed therein, lie receives all communications to the Assembly and superintends pll wiitings issued thence. If he will enter more into the discussions than is assigned to the functions of the Chairman, he must, meanwhile, resign the chair to the Vioc-Chairman. 7. In the Chairman's absence, the Vice-Chairman is fullv empowered, in every respect, to' preside in his stead. 8. The Secretary under the direction ol the Chairman, and aided by an assistant appointed by the Governor, keeps a compendious Protocol wherein the subjects of debate and their results are entered ; and these must at the commencement of the succeeding meeting he read to the Assembly both in Danish and English The Secretary collects the votes on a division of the house, after having first given his own. He also, under the direction of the Chairman, attends generally to what is expedited by the Assembly ; the expeditions must be signed by the Chairman and countersigned by the Secretary. $ 9. The Chairman at the close of every meeting, determines the order of the day for the ensuing one. Four Members of the Assembly, however, may demand that it be determined by a resolution of the Assembly. 10. The measures proposed to the Assembly by the Governor in behall of Government shall be communicated to the Assembly at

least 24 hours prior to the meeting, wherein it is to be decided how the measure is to be promoted, which can he done by immediately taking it up for preliminary discussion or else by referring it to a Committee for investigation. In order to promote the Asssembly's co-operation in the exorcise of legislative power, these matters, generally, ought to be discussed in preference to private ones, and it is the duty of the Chairman, in this respect, to do the needful. 5 11. If any Member intends to introduce a Bill in the Assembly, he must send in a memorial concerning it to the Chairman, written in duplicate, which always must contain a positive or definite proposal, and in as far as it aims at the issuing of a new law or ordinance must also contain a draft of such law or

ordinance. Thft Chairman has then to deliver one copy to the Governor, and at the same time by (posting) on a board made for this purpose, make the Assembly acquainted with the contents of the Bill On the day the Chairman may appoint, the mover of ihe Bill propounds it to the Assembly, which determine whether it shall be promoted ; if so, it can be done in either of the ways mentioned in the preceding paragraphs. At the close of each successive discussion, the Assembly decide whether the Bill is to progress further or not. 12. The Assembly can appoint standing Committees to which matters of a certain kind are to be referred ; also Committees for particular cases, unto which also subsequent new cases may be referred, when the subjects stand in connection with, or be allied to a previous one. In every stage of the discussion of a case, a Committee can be appointed, or the matter be sent for investigation to the Committee already appointed. The number of Members in a Committee may also be increased, and the Committee itself may call in one or more Membersby theconsentof the Assembly. The Committee appoints a Chairman to conduct its proceedings, and when that is done, a Speaker. 13. The meetings of a Committee ought to be so arranged as not to interfere with the meeting of its Members in the Assembly. No Member of a Committee should stay away from the meeting without sending to inform the Chairman of his being preveuted from attending. Matters in Committee ought to be furthered with all possible despatch.

Every deliberation and representation passed therein must be read at a meeting ol the Committee, and after being approved or corrected, signed by all the Members In case the Committee be not unanimous, the persons who differ in opinion from the majority are either to express their opinion in the report of the Committee, or else to attach their own views in a separate report, and conformably to that sign the report of the Committee. Upon which the report and the possible enclosure must be delivered to the Chairman of the Assembly, who must let it lie on the table of the same for the inspection of its Members for at least 48 hours before the subject is discussed. $ 14. On the subject being debated in the Assembly, it is the duly of the Speaker of the Committee to read the report of the Committee, and also the opinion of the dissenting Members. The subject is then to be taken up for the first or preliminary discussion. The Members during this must have the subject explained to them, and opportunities afforded them of becoming acquainted with the draft or proposal, and also with the dissentient opinions that might be expressed. During the discussion, every Member can, at any time, ask leave to speak ; demand explanations from the Speaker of the Committee, the Governor, or the mover of the motion, and also propose alterations and additions. 15. Amendments to a motion under discussion, must be introduced 48 hours ere they are taken in hand, on the second discussion spoken

of in 17. Proposals of altering amendments may be brought forward at the beginning of the meeting wherein these are discussed ; they must, however, be given in so betimes, that they, in a fitting manner, can be made known to the Assembly by the Chairman. A Committee has also the same right in respect to amendments, others, however, only when the Assembly exceptionally give their consent A motion to divide on any particular passage, an amendment, or the joining of two separate amendments under one voting, may even if it hns not previously been announced, be brought under consideration, but the motion must be announced before the discussion of the respective paragraphs, or amendments commences, and the Assembly thereunto give consent. 16. All motions or amendments can, in every stage be withdrawn, but they may also b«

D a ATI at1 immediately taken up by other Members of the Assembly. 17. On the second or the final discussion, which must not take place earlier than 3 times 24 hours after the close of the first discussion, the drafts or the motions with their appendant amendments are to be examined in such sections as the Chairman may find appropriate. Immediately after the discussion oi each section, or, in case the Chairman might deem it more suiiable, of the enure dralt or motion, the suffrages, in respect to them and the amendments relating thereto, are to be taken. lri respect to discussions, representations, and propositions suggested in tire Assembly, those solely, which have obtained majorities, are to be considered as valid ; the minority, however, alter the voting is finished on a second discussion, ate at liberty to demand their dissentient opinions together with the reasons, on which they are based, inserted in the report, representation or memorial which the Assembly intend to transmit to the Governor, or to the King through tiim. 18. After a case is decided, its final drawing up rests with the Committee or, if necessary, with the Secretary ; it must then be handed to (lie Chairman of the Assembly, who will cause it to be read so, that, it may be considered as finally passed, or if necessary, be corrected by the Assembly. 19 No one, with the exception of the Governor or his representative (Col: l.aw 24) and the Speaker, may on the second discussion of a Bill, speak moie than twice on a subject, or

on any minor section of the same, which separately may bebioughl under discussion, unless the Assembly give their consent. Addresses and similar communications to ' 20. the Assembly after being announced to them by the Chairman, are to be laid on the table of the Assembly without being read. Should the Chairman, or the Member, who received the address tor presentation, desire that, it may be read, the question of its being done is to be put to the vote, without discussion, at a subsequent meeting ; the reading thereof shall, however, only be allowed to take place, if three-fourths of the Members then present do agree to it. 21. If the Chairman finds that the discussions are unnecessat ily protracted, he can move their conclusion, which is to be decided by the Assembly without any discussion ; the Governor's or his representative's right to speak, however reserved according to the Col. Law 24 Four Members can likewise demand that it be put to the vote whether the debate shall be closed. The names of such Membets must be inserted in the Protocol. I 22. Every Member w ho lias asked and obtained leave to address the Assembly must speak from his place standing, and always address the Chairman. No one must either address his speech to another Member or call his name. ( 23. No speech must be read from a manuscript. . 24. The Member, who first rises will in general be given the preference to address the Assembly ; when several rise at the same time, the Chairman determines the order of speak-

ing. Preference may also be given to brief rectifications or to personal interrogations. As to the rest, speeches for and against a measure, should alternate. 25. Every Member is bound to submit to the decision of the Chairman respecting the maintenance of due order. The Chairman is authorised to interrupt or entirely break up the meeting in case circumstances render it necessary. 5 26. Significant expressions of approval or disapproval by the Members of the Assembly, are considered at variance with good order. 27. All questions excepting those spoken of in 20 and 31 are to be decided simply by a majority of votes. If the votes be equal, the

Chairman has to give his, but otherwise not. For each election more than one half the votes are requisite, and it is to be conducted conformably to the rules prescribed in 5. From this, however, are excepted the nominations of Members for Committees appointed by Ihe Assembly, for which one third of the votes shall be sufficient in as far as others have no more votes, F.very election ticket containing a greater or less number of names than are to be voted for, or a name insufficiently defined, or one that is not among the Members, is null and void. 28. The manner in which questions are to be put, is to be determined by the Chairman. At the request, however, of 4 Members, the Assembly may arrange it themselves after one of the 4 Members and the Speaker have expressed their opinion. 29. Voting in general takes place by rising from the seat, or by remaining sitting, ami the votes are to be counted by the Secretary. Should the Chairman be doubtful as to the result of the voting, it must be decided by calling the roll. This calling of the roll can also be demanded by 4 Members. Voting by Ballot takes place when 0 Members de mand it. The names of the Members, who demand the voting by roll or ballot, are to be entered into the Protocol. 5 30. Hindrances, whereby any one is prevented from meeting in the Assembly, must lie announced to the Chairman. Leave of absence, in as far as is consistent with the numerical strength of the Assembly, may be granted by the Chairman for 4 days, but if a longer

period is desired, the request must bo laid before the Assembly for decision. 31. On special pressing occasions, the preceding rules may be deviated from in as far as they are not based on the Regulations, contained in the Colonial Law þÿ when three fourths of Ihe voting Members agree.

New York Weekly Herald , August 7, 1852. By the arrival of the steamship Albatross, from Halifax, and by the telegraphic wires, we are enabled to lay before our readers a great deal of very interesting matter concerning the fishery difficulty with the British Provinces. Among other things, we observe that two vessels have already been fitted out at New Brunswick, for the express purpose of checking the encroachments of the French fishermen. It would thus appear that the Americans are not to be the only ones driven from the ground. Indeed, judging from the tone of the provincial press, as well as the official documents elsewhere given, the sole cause of the trouble with our neighbors on the other side of the St. Lawrence, was (heir anxious desire for reciprocal trade with us, combined with their opposition to the French fishermen. It will he seen that the inhabitants of the provinces are particularly desirous, in their petition to the Queen on the subject, that the Americans should continue to fish in (he waters thereabout; but, at the same time, they avoid alluding to the French, from whom they derive no advantage in the way of trade; while, on the other hand, it is a well established tact that they reap many perquisites from the Americans, by the sale of produce, the right of curing fish on shore, Ate., in addition to which a very large number of them gain a livelihood by being employed on board of our vessels. They seem to understand perfectly well that the withdrawal of the American fishermen from their coasts will really

be an almost insurmountable loss to them. This fishery affair was the cause of considerable discussion, and no little excitement, in the United States Senate on Tuesday þÿ a message having been received from the President, transmitting all the official correspondence appertaining thereto. Our Senators evince a determination not to be driven in this matter, come what may, and will oppose any treaty touching reciprocity in trade, or anything else, on the part of the Executive, that will in any way interfere with the rights of the legislative branch of the government concerning the regulation of the revenue laws. The speeches of Messrs. Cass, Davis and Hamlin, on this subject, are particularly striking, and will be read with attention. The reader will elsewhere find accounts of the progress and ravages of the cholera throughout the country. Although the disease is unusually malignant, it is pleasing to know that it does not prevail to within anything like the extent it did in former years, and that most of the cases occur in isolated instances, where there is a want of proper ventilation and cleanliness. The malady has already rapidly diminished in Buffalo and Rochester, and will probably entirely disappear from those places in a few days. The yellow fever was 6till prevailing with great fatality at Port au Prince, and other ports in the island of Hayti, on the 16th ult. Owing to the news of the bad vintage all kinds of French brandies in France, brought out by the and Europa, wines
have met with large speculative sales, within the past few days.

To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Dear Sir, I have seen your remarks oil my views respecting the prudence and propriety ot tho People returning men in the pay and employ of Government, Representatives in the Colonial Assembly, and I am as their not at all astonished, that you do not sec matters in the same light in which I view them, for men will differ in their opinions and much good frequently results from such differences. But 1 do not tlnnk, that mv views will be considered by impartial men as unsound, or even biased by party-spirit, because they meet v<»"r approbation. An exchange of ideas is do not always useful, whether no offence it takes place in a friendly manner. I at having party-spirit in public or private, provided attributed therefore take to me, as 1 certainly know myself free of it, unless you designate

as such my wish Not to see Government Officers " sfi the Representatives in the Colonial Assembly, otherwise I maintain that no party-spirit appears in my remarks, as stated by you in your Paper of 17th instant. Respecting your views of the meetings for in what trialmanner they have been directly beneficial, votings, I would request you to point out, and how far their proposed end « To prevent canvassing and biasing of opinions" has been accomplished. If you cannot do so, my assertion holds good, that these meetings were unnecessary and have not answered their proposed purpose. þÿ I cannot admit, that your want of information on the subject of canvassing for votes, or biasing of opinions privately, is or a proof, that in such practice is not going on directly indirectly, the towns as well as in the country ; on the contrary the tact is too well known, to require any further proot. I admire much the firm spirit you attribute to the Townvoters; but their being possessed of such I spirit, is no reason why they should not take the views have offered, into consideration, and if after mature deliberation these prove sound, also follow them. The first paragraph reads as follows : þÿ There shall be erected for the Danish West India Possessions a Colonial Assembly, invested in the manner ordained hereafter, with a deliberative voice with regard to the exercise of the legislative power. þÿ On the motion of the Colonial Assembly, the King may decree its division into two Assemblies, the one for Saint Croix, and the other for Saint Thomas and Saint Johns, for the transaction of all business, or of some particular branches, and make the provisions required by this alteration in the present þÿ The seventh paragraph directs that þÿLaw.1 þÿ The Colonial Assembly consists of 16 members elected by the people, viz, 8 for St. Croix, 6 for St. Thomas, and 2 for St. Johns; and of 4 members appointed by the þÿKing. THE FOLLOWING ADDRESS was presented to the þÿRev d. Mr. Butler, Rector of the Catholic Church, Christiansted, on the eve of his departure from this Island. Much esteemed and respected Pastor! The sad moment for your departure having unfortunately too soon arrived, we hasten to manifest our sorrow at the cause of your leaving us, and to express the hope, that a change of climate will prove conducive to the restoration of that health so valuable to each and every one of us. It would be vain for us to attempt to describe our feelings on this occasion; suffice it for us to hope that they are reciprocated, Dear Reverend, by you. This alone will enable us to indulge the pleasing expectation that you will not forsake us entirely, but that when it pleases God to give you back that lost health you will not refuse to return among those who will ever be ready to give you a warm and affectionate welcome. We now beg leave to appeal to your own feelings; can you look on that sacred Edifice which has caused you so much labour and anxiety þÿ at the pleasing spectacle which the interior presents to your view, in the numerous congregation therein assembled to assist at the celebration of the Divine Mysteries, and to profit of the good instructions delivered to them, þÿ and yet feel satisfied that another should enjoy those fruits which have cost you ten and a half years of arduous labour? This would be a very great sacrifice, indeed, nor are we satisfied that it should be so.

We cannot deny but that during your sojourn among us, you have had many crosses and difficulties to encounter ; the like, unfortunately, are to be met with every where ; but we cherish the hope, that the good feeling and sympathy of your people, have contributed to lighten, at least, the weight of your burden. In conclusion, we beg leave to tender you our warmest thanks for your earnest solicitude for our spiritual welfare, and that the Almighty God may pour down his choicest blessings on you þÿ grant you a prosperous voyage þÿ and a speedy recovery, are the sincere and earnest wishes of Your devoted and » ere follow the signatures. affectionate parishioners. »»> þÿ Tin Rcv'il. .Hr. Ruder' Reply.

My dearly beloved friends and children in Jesus Christ ! Permit me, to thank you, with all the warmth of a deeply grateful heart, for the very kind and flattering address, which you have been pleased to present to me. When 1 look back to the day, on which 1 first came amongst you ; and look forward to the near approaching day, which is to separate me from you ; 1 confess my anxiety is very great: and the heavy feelings, which oppress my heart, cannot be conveyed to you in words. If, during my residence amongst you, I have contributed in any way to your spiritual welfare, and to the progress of our holy religion ; 1 cannot claim the merit altogether to myself. In you my good and indulgent people, l have always found the ready means of assistance þÿ to cooperate with me þÿ to forward my views, and to bear with me my burden and the heat of the day. Faithful as you have been during the past, may I not hope, as my greatest comfort and consolation, that you will be faithful for the future. Firmly convinced as I am, that neither time nor space, nor things present or things to come, will ever change your pious sentiments ; 1 commend to your especial care, the church, which you have built þÿ I commend to you the poor and the sick, watch over them as the special friends and favourites of Him, who was the outcast of the world. I commend myself also to your prayers þÿ and yourselves, one and all, I commend to the especial protection of God, and the patronage of her, to whom were addres-

Johnson, of tl.e Rifle þÿBrigade was ordered to Canada with his battalion, in which he was then a captain, and being very fond of falconry, to which he had devoted much time and expense, he took with him two of his favorite peregrines, as his companions, across the Atlantic. þÿ It was his constant habit during the voyage to allow them to fly every day after þÿ feeding them þÿup, that they might not be induced to rake off after a passing sea-gull, or wander out of sight of the vessel. Sometime their rambles were very wide and protracted. At others they would ascend to such a height as to bo

almost lost to the view of the passengers, who soon found them an effectual means of relieving the tedium of a long sea voyage, and naturally took a lively interest in their welfare ; but as they were in the habit of returning regularly to the ship, no uneasiness was felt during their occasional absence. At last, one evening, after a longer flight than usual, one of the falcons returned alone. The þÿother the prime favorite þÿ was missing. Day after day passed away, and, however much he may have continued to regret his loss, Captain Johnson had at length fully made up his mind that it was irretrievable, and that he should never see her again. Soon after the arrival of the regiment in America, on casting his eyes over a Halifax newspaper, he was struck by a paragraph announcing that the captain of an American shooner had at that moment in his possession a find hawk, which had suddenly made its appearance on boad his ship during his late passage from Liverpool. The idea at once occurred to Captain Johnson that this could be no other than his much-prized falcon, so having obtained immediate leave of absence, he set off for Halifax, a journey of some days. On arriving there he lost no time in waiting on the commander of the schooner, announcing the object of his journey, and requested that he might be allowed to see the bird ; but Jonathan had no idea of relinquishing his prize so easily, and stoutly refused to admit of the interview, þÿ guessing þÿ that it was very

easy for an Englisher to lay claim to another þÿman s property, but þÿ calculating þÿ that it was a þÿ tarnation sight harder for him to get possession of it ; and con þÿ eluded by asserting, in unqualified terms, his entire disbelief in the whole story. Captain þÿJohnson o s bject, however, being rather to recover his falcon than to pick a quarred with the truculent Yankee, he had fortunately sufficient self-command to curb his indignation, and proposed that his claim to the ownership of the bird should be at once put to the test by an experiment, which several Americans who were present admitted to be perfectly reasonable, and which their countryman was at last persuaded to acquiesce. It was this. Captain Johnson was to be admitted to an interview with the þÿhawk who, by the way, had as yet shown no partiality for any person since her arrival in the New World ; but, on the contrary, had rather repelled all attemps at familiarity þÿ and if at this meeting she should not only exhibit such unequivocal signs of attachment and recognition as should induce the majority of the bystanders to believe that he really was her original master, but especially if she should play with the buttons of his coat, then the American was at once to waive all claim to her. The trial was immediately made. The Yankee went up-stairs, and shortly returned with the falcon ; but the door was hardly opened before she darted from his fist, and perched at once on the shoulder of her beloved and long-

lost protector, evincing, by every means in her power, her delight and affection, rubbing her head against his cheek, and taking hold of the buttons of his coat and champing them playfully between her mandibles, one after another. This was enough. The jury were unanimous. A verdict for the plaintiff was pronounced ; even the obdurate heart of the sea-captain was melted, and the falcon was at once restored to the arms of her rightful owner.

THE QUEEN'S SPEECH. HOUSE OF þÿlords. Thursday, July 1. Parliament was dissolved this day by her Majesty in person. The weather was fine, but the number of persons along the line of procession unusually small. Her Majesty left Buckingham Palace a few minutes before two o'clock, and entered the House at twenty

<© 1£ SI AT!! 3 minutes past, when, the Commons having been summoned, her Majesty delivered the following speech: þÿ My Lords and Gentlemen, I am induced by considerations of public policy to release you at an earlier period than usual from your legislative duties. The zeal and diligence, however, with which you have applied yourselves to youi parliamentary labours have enabled me in the comparatively short session to give my assent to many measures of high importance, and 1 trust of great and permanent advantage. 1 receive from all foreign powers assurances that they ate animated by the most friendly dispositions towards this country; and 1 entertain a confident hope that the amicable relations happily subsisting between the firmly principal European States may Provi- established as, under Divine tie so dence, to secure to the world a long continuance of the blessings of peace ; to this great end my attention will be unremittingly directed. 1 rejoice that the final settlement of the affairs of Holstein and Schleswig, by the general concurrence of the poweis chiefly interested, has removed one cause of lecent difference and of future anxiety. The amicable termination to the dissensions which have taken place between the Sublime Porte and the Faslia of Egypt allord a guarantee for the tranquility ol I he East, and encouragement to the extension of commercial enterprise. The refusal on the part of the King of Avn, of redress, justly demanded for insults and injuries offered to my subjects at Ban-

goon, has necessarily led to an interruption of friendly relations with that sovereign. The promptitude and vigour with which the Governor-General ol India lias taken the measures rendered unavoidable, have merited my entire approbation; and 1 am confident that vou will participate in ttie satisfaction with which I have observed the conduct of all the naval and military foices, European and Indian. by whose valour and discipline the important captures of Rangoon and Martaban have been accomplished, and in the hope which 1 entertain that these signal successes may lead to an early and honourable peace. Treaties have been concluded by my naval commanders with the King of Dahomey, and all the African chiefs, whose rule extends along the Bight of Benin, for the total abolition of the slave trade, which is at present wholly suppressed upon that coast. 1 have had great satisfaction in giving my assent to the measures which you have adopted lor the better organization of ilie mililia. A constitutional force which, being limited to purposes of internal defence, can afford no just ground jealousy of to neighbouring powers ; but which, in the event ot any sudden and unforeseen disturbance ol my foreign relations, would contribute eventually to the protection and security of my dominions. Gentlemen of the House of Commons, 1 thank you for the liberal provisions which you have made for the exigencies of the public service. The expenditure which you have authorised shall be applied with a due

regard to economy and efficiency. The recent discoveries of extensive gold fields have produced in the Australian colonies a temporary disturbance of society requiring prompt attention 1 have taken such steps as appeared to me most urgently necessary for the mitigation of this serious evil. I shall continue anxiously to watch the important results which must follow from these discoveries. 1 have willingly concurred with you in anv act which, by rendering available to the services of those colonies the portion arising within them of the hereditary revenue placed at the disposal of Parliament on my accession to the throne, may enable them to meet their necessarily increased expenditure. My Lords and Gentlemen, 1 have gladly assented to the important bills which you have passed for effecting re-

forms, long and anxiously desired, in the practice and proceedings of the superior Courts of Law and Equity, and generally for improving the administiation of justice. Every measure which simplifies the forms, and diminishes the delay and expenses of legal proceedings, without introducing uncertainty of decision, impairing the authority of the courts, or lowering the high standard of the judicial bench, is a valuable boon conferred upon the Community at large. 1 hope that the measures which you have adopted for promoting the extramural interment of the dead, and for improving the supply of water, may be found effectual for the remedy of evils, the existence of which has long been a reproach to this great metropolis, and may conduce to the health and comfort of its inhabitants. The extension of popular rights and legislative power to mv subjects residents in the colonies is always to me an object of deep interest, and I trust that their pieseot native institutions, which, in concert w ith you 1 have sanctioned for New Zealand, may promote the welfare and contentment of the population of that distant but most interesting colony, and confirm their loyalty and attachment to my crown. It is my intention, without delay, to dissolve this present Parliament; and it is my earnest prayer that, in the exercise of the high functions which, according to our free constitution, they may he directed by an allwise Providence to the selection of representatives whose wisdom and patriotism may

aid me in mv increasing erufeavouis to sustain the honour and dignity of my crown, to uphold the Protestant institutions of the country, and the civil and religious liberty which is their natural result, to extend and improve the national education, to develope and encourage industry and science, and to elevate the moral and social condition, and thereby promoto the welfare and happiness of my people. »««- WEST INDIA SI GAIC.

General Scott. Long ere this the lightning has informed a large portion of the inhabitants of the United States that Gen. Scott has been chosen as the whig candidate for the Presidency. House's printing telegraph succeeded in furnishing us with the first announcement; hut, at the same moment, the various other lightning lines were busily engaged in disseminating the information in all directions. There are some curious and unparalleled incidents connected with the proceedings of the Whig and Democratic Conventions. þÿ Both bodies were in session five days. The democrats had forty-nine and the whigs fifty-three ballots before they succeeded in effecting a choice; hut then the former had to decide between the claims of upwards of eight or ten prominent candidates, while the latter had only three. However, the whigs made up for their disparity of candidates for the Presidency when they came to ballot for Vice President, for which office, on the first trial, votes were thrown for no less than eighteen different gentlemen.

The Independence of San Juan þÿ Very Important. þÿ This event, which will he found announced in our news today, is one of great importance both to England and the United States. For several years this has been a hone of contention between the two countries, and a source of bitterness and had feeling. The difficulty, which was increased by the demand of the right of way for the Nicaragua canal, is now entirely removed. Everything amicably is settled. The independence of San Juan is agreed to, and the canal will he immediately constructed. The merchants of London, on condition of the political event which has now taken place, and the surveys of Col. Childs, certifying the practicability of the work, agreed to take thirty millions of dollars worth of the stock, or one-half of the entire. Colonel Childs, having made the surveys, is now gone

to England ; and the independence of San Juan being established, nothing remains to interfere with the completion of the work. This is a matter of vast importance to the commercial world, in the old country and the new ; and the amicable arrangement of differences is much better for all parties concerned than the exploded arguments of powder and hall. þÿ Ibid.

The government papers of the city ol Mexico, on the 19th of May, contain an official proposition, signed by President Arista and his officers, announcing his willingness to enter into a contract to promote the formation of a company to construct a railroad, canal, or wagon road across the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, subject to the approval of the Mexican Congress. Preference is avowed to the work being done by a congress of nations, but, in any event, Mexico is to retain its sovereignty over the Isthmus. The parties taking the contract shall guarantee the freedom of the road to all nations. The Mexican government will bind itself to negotiate with foreign powers to recognise the neutrality of the right of way accross the Isthmus. Having completed liis work, Antiquitates Americana!, Ratii undertook in connection with Finn Magnusen the preparation and publication, on behalf nt the Society, of another work relating to the Ante-Columbian age of America, the Historical Monuments of Greenland, which was issued in three volumes with twelve plates 1838 and 1845. In this work the deceased Finn Magnusen had an important share and contributed to it many valuable articles ; an account of the later voyages which have had lor their object the re-discovery of this polar land was communicated by l)r. C. I'nigel. The Secretary Charles C. Rain conducted a correspondence with several active public officers in the land itself, who in the ten years from 1833 to 1841 undertook antiquarian tours at the expense of the Society and also made excavations and examinations of the numerous ruins which exist there, the results of which are communicated in the work. Rafn appended a view of the ancient geography of Greenland. A third work relating to America, which will be much more extensive, is already commenced, namely : lslendinga Sogur, the ancient historical writings of Iceland, of which the first two volumes have been issued, the editing of the original old Danish or old Icelandic text being executed by John Sigurdssou. SCANDINAVIAN SOURCES OF THE HISTORY OF THE EAST. Meanwhile, Charles C. Rafn, during the twelve years since 1839, has been chiefly engaged in the preparation of another work, in imp. 4to, of which the

lirst volume is now ready and the second about half printed, namely, Antiquites Russcs et Orientales d'aprcs les monuments historiqueB des Islandais et des anciens Scatidiuaves. This work, for which also communications are promised, and in part received, from various fellow - laborers (Icelanders, Norwegians, Swedes and Danes) is intended to comprise the following sections: 1, Extracts from the old inythico-historical writings, 2, Extracts from the ancient historical writings, which constitute the most important section of

f the work, from the Sagas, from the Icelandic Annals and from the old Geographical writings. 3, Runic inscriptions which make mention of the Varags in Russia or the Vie rings in Greece. 4, Deeds and other public papers of the middle ages written in one of the Northern languages before the end of the 14th century. The text is accompanied by translations in Latin and by introductions and comments in French, and is illustrated by fac-similes of the most important manuscripts which have been used, and by plates of the runic stones etc. GUIDE TO NORTHERN ARCHAEOLOGY. The Earl of Ellesinere, for the use of English readers has published, London 1848, a new translation of the Society's Guide to Northern Archaeology, to which is also appended an account of the works which had been issued by the Society, up to that time, noticing also the Antiquitates Americana; and the various books, treatises .etc. to which that work has given rise (p. 1 12- 120). Besides this work, by which the Earl of Ellesmere has sought to extend the English reader's acquaintance with Northern archaeology and ancient history, the Society owes him and his brother, the Duke of Sutherland, its acknowledgements for the readiness with which they both promoted the antiquarian investigations of Mr. Worsaae, a Danish archaeologist and an active member of the Society, in Scotland and the Scottish Islands. PERIODICAL WORKS ON NORTHERN AR- CHAEOLOGY AND HISTORY. The Society lias continued the publication of its

periodical works, comprising dissertations and contributions tending to elucidate the archaiology, ancient history and geography, jurisprudence and philology of the North. The Mr moires des Antiquaires du Nord contain treatises and communications in French, English or German ; the Antiquarisk Tidsskrift in Icelandic, Swedish or Danish. Three years of the latter constitute a volume. Resides these, a volume of more extended essays in one of the three last-named languages Annaler for nordisk Oldkyndighed og Historie, Annals of Northern Archamlogy and History, is issued annually. These publications, illustrated with a num- so ber of steel engravings and lithographs, have been fortunate as to win by degress an extended recognition as being, what in their origin they were intended to become, the chief organ for Northern arehamlogy and for the earlier history of the North prior to the introduction of the Reformation, as well as the organ lor the communications of the Northern, that is, the Icelandic, Norwegian, Swedish and Danish archseologists and historical investigators. In the Earl of Ellesniere's above-mentioned Guide may be found a specification of the contents of the earlier volumes of these Annals prior to 1847. The "AVIS." Christianstod, Tuesday the 27tli of July 1852. In re-publishing the translation of a Memorial to the Diet, in which the former slave -owners remonstrate against the small sum of $ 40 offered as compensation for each slave emancipated in 1848, we beg leave to state, that the translation which appeared in our paper of the 10th instant does not convey correctly the substance of the original document. The Memorial itself is at the Burgher Council's Office, open for signatures, until the 12th of next month, when the same will be forwarded to Copenhagen. We hope, that no person who has suffered by the Emancipation Act of 3d July 1848 will omit to sign the petition.

To tlic Vict. The undersigned inhabitants of the Island of St. Croix, who, on the 3rd July 1848, were slave-owners, have the honour of addressing the Danish Diet with a petition tending to secure its assistance in obtaining the compensation, they consider themselves entitled to, in consequence of the emancipation of their slaves. After we, in the distress this event had reduced us to, and which to many amongst us involved the loss of all their property, had repeatedly addressed llis Majesty the King and the Ministry of Finances, as entrusted with the direction of the Colonies, with petitions for such compensation, without thereby attaining any result, the Ministry has at length laid before the last Diet the draft of a law, granting compensation to the former owners of slaves in these Colonies, but so late, that the Diet could not find time to proceed further in the matter than to a preliminary discussion. It is to be exsubject pected, that the draft will be in made of further deliberation the the impending Diet, and we must therefore not neglect both to recommend our cause to the same, and also to point out the little satisfactory manner, in which the conve- try in the said draft has thought Minisnient to despatch our claim, which, refusing to acknowledge as a legal one, still at the same time admits to be founded on equity and justice. We cannot admit as valid, the distinction drawn by the Ministry and several members of the last Diet, between the right of property in slaves, and that in

other goods, so far as the conclusion is concerned which this distinction is to lead to, in regard to the compensation question. In this respect tjie distinction is void of all legal and practical foundation, and the restrictions in the exercise of the right of property, upon which one has based such a distinction, and which one very incorrectly styles restrictions of the right itself, can neither according to general legal notions, nor according to analogies derived from the limitations, to which the use of almost all other kinds of property is subjected, nor to common reason, be of any effect when the question of indemnification for an abolished right of property is discussed. Any right of property is, regarding its exercise, limited by certain necessary and rational bounds, which of course must and do vary according to the object being either an inanimate and irrational one or a human creature. But, we repeat, this restriction affects merely the exercise of the right, not its essence and substance, and has no force but in its express and rational tendency to regulate the use of such a right, as long as it exists. The

3 V% <0 IK © a X AT1! 3. greater or less, the more general or more I particular limitation of a right is a fact, which ceases to exist with the right itself, and which, as long as it existed, was one of the agents, that served to fix its value in commerce. When the right ceases, it ceases with the value, which was determined by the restriction, and the latter can not naturally, after having accomplished its effect, be called upon again to affect a value, which it previously had already served to fix. Thus this value is no other but the identical one, with which the property was invested at the time of the abolition of the right. It is easy to determine the same, the more so, as it can be demonstrated by the valuation of slaves, fixed and revised, by the Government and the Burgher Council, for the purpose of regulating compulsory sales effecting selfliberation, and moreover by the prices obtained by the Royal Treasury itself for the slaves, belonging or mortgaged to the same, which were sold even up to a period, shortly preceding emancipation. It is but right here to remark, that the Royal Treasury has at all times participated in all such transactions, the object ot which was purchasing, selling, mortgaging slaves, that it yet is in possession of bonds, stipulating expressly the right of mortgage not only in landed properties with their inventory of slaves, but even in the persons of slaves, that are unconnected with any such property, and that the said Treasury now most rigorously calls upon its delitors to pay the

capital together with 0 per cent interest, due for purchased slaves, refusing even to comply with the often-repeated petition, to grant delay for further payments until after a final settlement of the compensation question. The Ministry, in refusing to acknowledge our legal claim to compensation, has thrown out this assertion without any proof. And such proof cannot be adduced. It may be tempting, when any one by a public position is necessitated to make a proposition, the unpopularity of which he is aware of, to proclaim, that the weaker part, that would be benefited by the same, has in fact no legal claim to get anything, and thus to exhibit bis feeling of equity and justice, for, what he under such a supposition agrees to give, he accords from mere generosity and at the same time gains the power of arbitrarily fixing the amount of the gift. But in order to maintain such a position, one must prove it, or, what is the same, prove, that there did not exist any right of property over slaves, and this would be nothing else, but to prove what is in itself contradictory. Our whole legislature, as far as it regards the Colonies, acknowledges slaves as legal property, the whole social order in the Colonies is based upon slavery as a matter of right, existing de jure and de facto, and the particular restrictions, which the exercise of the right of property over slaves must be subject to, do not, as we above have proved, affect the right itself. Now it is a principle, acknowledged and

established in the whole Danish just as well as in the legislature of all other civilized nations, that the right of property is sacred and inviolable, and that it cannot be abolished but where the common weal required it, and even then only with full compensation. In further corroboration of this truth we can not only adduce the contents of a Placard, dated 31st July 18(11, but with special reference to the West Indies the law of 3rd April 1755, 34, according to which the owner is to be compensated for the slave sentenced to death ; the law of 1st May 1840, resolving, that the owners of slaves should be obliged to give up their right of property for full compensation.

In regard to an argument, used by the Mother Country against our claim to compensation, viz : that the Rescript ot 28th July 1847 had fixed a term for the expiration of slavery, we have simply to observe, that the said Rescript passed over the compensation-question and left it undecided and that already in the first meeting of the commission, appointed for the purpose of making propositions for carrying into effect the contents of the Rescript, the members urged the claim of compensation, to be enforced together with the emancipation. It would however in itself be useless to adduce this Rescript, which was partly looked upon as 'little suitable, partly remained a dead letter, and which, it really put into execution, would have created a miserable and intolerable condition in the Colonies. It has amongst other arguments been maintained, (and, so far as we have been able to learn, even from this very Island,) that the slave owners had suffered no loss by emancipation, and therefore had no claim to compensation. From the same source has been urged, that slavery could not exist any longer, because it had outlived itself, and that emancipation was only a formal corroboration of this result. Common sense, will, we trust, dispense with our refuting all the garbled statements and arguments, which emanate from people, that arc devoid either of good will, or the capacity of judging of the public relations of" the community, they live in, in an impartial and rational manner. It it thus must be acknowledged, that

we had a legal right of property in our slaves, that this right was annulled against our will, and through no fault of ours, and that we have thereby sustained severe losses, it is palpable, that we are entitled to full compensation from the. Slate. But full compensation is verv d liferent from the one offered by the Ministry. Full compensation is' the market price ot the slave at the time of emancipation. If, in order to avoid practical difficulty and a further delay, which would be unfair to us, an equitable average price be fixed for each slave, we can have no objection. But instead of that we are offered $40 in bonds, which we could not even realize, which are to be cancelled in the course of 13 years, and only bear 4 per cent interest, to begin from the fourth anniversary of the destruction of our property. Such a bond would, as the legal percentage here is (5 per cent, only be realized at a loss of at least 20 per cent, so that we instead of $40 would in reality only receive $32 lor a slave, and besides lose 4 years' interest or 24 per cent of the capital. Such a settlement, were it even a mere claim of justice and equity, appears to us neither just nor eqyitablc. The financial position of the Mother Country has been urged as an impediment against granting us a compensation adequate to the full value of our slaves. That it in justice and equity can demand of us, that we should allow some influence on the amount of compensation and the form of disbursement to this incontrover-

tible fact we willingly concede, though this argument appears not to have exercised any influence on the amount of indemnification fixed for damages of war or the equalization of privileged and unprivileged lands. But, in allowing such a concession to be made, we must still militate against the unfairness of the ministerial proposition, and we do hereby with unlimited confidence recommend our just cause to the chosen representatives of the Danish nation and thus we seek our right, where right was never denied.

( Continued.) of A DESIGNATION FOR THE ANCIENT LANGUAGE OF THE NORTH. In the Introduction lo the Earl of Ellesmere's abovementioned Guide to Northern Archteolocry, p. XIII- XVI, will be found some observations, "rounded upon extracts from the old writings, upon a designation for the ancient language of the North which deserve especial attention. The language which in ancient times prevailed over the whole North was called, at first, in Iceland as well as in the rest of the North, donsk tunga, Danish tongue. In the younger or Snorre's Edda it is mentioned in this manner (Arna-Magn. ed,. vol. I, p. 374) : "Because the Danish King, Frode was the most powerful of all the Kings in the Northern lands (a Noriirlbndum), the peace prevailing in his time was called from him throughout the whole Danish language (uin alia danska tungu) and was styled by the Northmen (Noromenn) the peace of Frode." This common language had also the same designation in Su -alen (see Ynglinga Saga chap. 20) as well as in Norway, in the oldest historical period, as is seen from various excellent parchments (Fornnanna Siigur III p. 10, 37; IV, p. 73; V, 357 ; X, p. 179, 364). Of the Skalds of Har.ild the Fair-haired, the first absolute monarch of Norway, it is said that they repaid his gifts " w ith such words of eulogy as will never be forgotten so long as the Danish language endures." Of Olaf Tryggvason Odd Monk says that he was the most celebrated man " of the Danish tongue a danska tungul." Of Earl Hakon, the son of Erik

he was of the best race " of the Danish tongue ; and and grandson of Hakon, the Skald Sighvat says that of St. Olaf the Priest Einar Skularson says that this prince's prudence was the greatest of all "in the Danish language". This designation for the tongue is thus connected with four of the most celebrated characters of Norway's older history. Donsk tunga occurs also as the designation for the common language of the Northmen in the narratives of their jourines in foreign lands ; for example, in England, in Italy namely in Roma and Lucca, in Syria Fornmanna Nijgur, III, p. 37; VI, p, 401 ; XI, p. 202,301, and for that of the Varags in Russia and id' the Wrings in Constantinople, Katu's Antiquitcs Russcset Orientate t. II, p. 151 1 Later, about the period of the 13th century, the name norrama was used, not exclusively for Norwegian but for Northern in general. Norramn signifies, originally Northerly. Northern, and is formed just as the adjectives austra nn, suroamn, vestnenn are for the other cardinal points; norraena also means North wind see Rain's Antiquitutes Ann ricun.T p. 21. This extended signification of norrtenn can he seen from a remarkable parchment fragment Fornmanna Sdgur XI, p. 412 in which it is said ; ' The beginning of all veracious legends i norrainni tiingu is at the time when the Ases settled in the North Nordritj, for it is truly said that this language which we call norrania came with them here to the North, and tiiis tongue has spread over Saxony, Denmark and Sweden, Norway

and a part of England." In this meaning the adjective norrsenn is especially taken when it is used in opposition lo anotiier language outside of the Scandinavian North, such as German which is said of the German (Suromaor) Tyrker who followed Leif Erik son on his voyage of discovery to America in the year 1000, Irish (Antiq. Ann r. p. 45. 217-249; Grunlands historiske Mindesmairker 11, 66) ; French and Flemish (Saga of Lawrence, Rishop of Holar, chap. 8), the languages of the Permians, Rafn's Antiquitcs Russes et Orientates t. I, p. 100, Greek girzk or griksk, ib. t. II p. 69. Afterwards, however, the adjective was used in the limited signification of Norwegian, in which sense it often occurs, according to the same transition of meaning, from a more extended signification to a more confined one, which the substantives Noroinenn and Nororlond have undergone. Noromenn originally signified collectively the Scandinavian inhabitants of the North, the Norlhmanni of the Latin writers; but afterwards, when the signification prevailing in the more southerly situated Denmark became dominant, it was used exclusively of Norwegians, the inhabitants of Norw ay ; Nororlimd, which every where in the ancient writings is used of .the Northern lands in general, is employed now only of provinces in Northern Norway Nordlaudene, and Sweden, Norrland. The Icelanders thus called in the oldest period the language common to them and the whole North, Danish, donsk tunga, and afterwards styled it fre-
quently norrirn. First, in a far later time, when the language in the rest of the North had become so

; T. C 1$ 0 J 2 AYl changed that the ancient tongue ceased to be understood there, it was called Icelandic, because it was then confined to the island of Iceland alone, where this identical tongue lias been preserved almost unchanged to our days, so that the common people yet read with interest the Sagas and such other ancient writings as are adapted to their comprehension and sphere of knowledge, even the historical lays and songs of the Edda, which were undoubtedly composed in Denmark, Sweden and Norway. Collateral to these designations, the philologist Rask and the Northern Antiquaries have introduced the comprehensive and peculiarly characteristic term Old Northern, which so exactly denotes what it should denote, as the language as well as the literature is unquestionably the common property of the whole North, although Iceland is the country to which the merits of both its custody and preservation are due. This designation has now gained a right of citizenship both in the Danish, oldnordisk, and Swedish, fornnordisk, and lias been also adopted by German and English authors; it is also to be preferred to the term Norse which was formerly used in the Scottish islands, and to all other designations, if the oldest name Danish which, as the oldest, has the greatest claim, should not be adopted. The "AVIS." Christiansted, Friday the 30th of July 1852. As the time approaches for the election of members to sit in the Colonial Council, we understand, much earnest canvassing is going on throughout the country, and we are sorry -to learn that, in some instances, undue influences are brought to bear, perhaps, not amounting to intimidation, but which are powerful enough to control that free, unshackled, and independent choice of Representatives, which every man, having the right to vote, ought to be able to exercise according to his own will and conviction, and not at the dictation of another, be he proprietor or attorney. Touching this point we would in the most friendly, yet forcible manner, remind Managers that their employers hire their services, which they cannot do without, and not their opinions, which they have no right to control or direct in such matters ; and we say this, notwithstanding it was asserted, we hear, by one of the " magnets" a short time since, at a certain "Congress of nominators" (who, we opine, reckoned a little without their host) that managers were bound, he thought, to vote for such persons as they directed, and in fact suggested that planters should desire their managers to insert the names of those for whom they intended to vote in their weekly reports, in juxtaposition, no doubt, with the mules and horned cattle, like which, they probably anticipated driving in flocks their pliant dependents to the poll. In favorable contrast, however, to the above, if true, we feel bound as faithful

journalists, to mention the liberal conduct of an attorney þÿ the truth of which we can vouch for þÿ who told the managers under him to vote for whom they thought proper þÿ that he did not even wish to know for whom they intended voting; this is as it should be, and we think does much credit to the gentleman we allude to. We, therefore, confidently trust that managers will act firmly in repelling such attempts, if made, and resolutely maintain their independence, and show that they both feel and know their own respectability and importance as a portion of the community of this Island, and not submit to be made the tools of any aspirants, from fear, favor, or affection, nor be led to vote for thosevhom they do not fully believe to be in possession of the necessary qualifications to fulfill, efficiently, the duties which such a position involves; but to give their support, only, to those whom they believe, above all, to have the liberality and determination to promote, as far as in their power, impartially and equally the interest of all classes ; principles which, it is obvious, it is the duty of every man to support, and without possessing which, no man should have a voice in the Colonial Council. Objections have been made, by some timid people, to the mode of voting, viva voce, in accordance with the 17th $ of the Colonial Law ; but it only requires a little resolution in Voters to do what is right, and, in fact, what their obligations as citizens demand of them, to overcome

this difficulty. We cannot but regret this apparent defect in the law, and hope it will very soon be remedied ; for it certainly must be considered as placing an unwholesome restraint upon the free exercise of men's votes, because it may, and in fact will, have the effect of inducing some individuals to vote contrary to their own inclination and judgment, while others may remain away and forego the privilege of voting at all, rather than run the risk of injuring their private interests or of offending personal friends.

The Colonial Law, as it now stands, may not be all that we could wish; like all human institutions it requires time and experience to improve and make it what it ought to be þÿ more suitabletoour wants; but it is a step in the right direction, and it very much depends upon ourselves whether it shall turn out to be a blessing to the Colony or the reverse. If men are returned, who from sectional feelings, or private interest, are incapable of taking a broad view of matters, and thereby clog the wheels of legislation ; we can expect or look for very little benefit to flow from it, at least, for some time to come.

The French Eagles ! late presentation of the " Eagles" to the Regiments in A distinguished French Officer, in allusion to the Paris, communicates the following sanguinary episode which proves the extent of devotion shewn by the brave soldiers to its colours. At the battle of Austerlitz, the 4th Regiment of the line having advanced with too much impetuosity in the midst of the enemy, experienced the loss of the entire First Batallion þÿ cut to pieces by the Russian Imperial Cavalry, and its Eagle captured þÿ the Eagle bearer, St. Cyr., receiving fourteen sabre wounds, and the two subaltern officers, acting assistant Eagle-bearers, were also killed. Altho' this gallant regiment wrenched four standards from their enemies on that day, the Emperor did not pardon it for having lost its Eagle ; and it was only after the battle of Jena, and in consequence of the prayers and entreaties of the generals and superior officers of that corps, that he consented to allow it a new one, which interesting circumstance took place at a review at Berlin. Having stationed himself in the centre of tlie square formed by the 4th of the line, he addressed to them a fiery harangue, concluding with these empha- tic words, " I would prefer to lose my right arm rather than to see the Eagle of France full into the hands of its enemies." On the eve of the battle of Eylaw, in 1807, the 4th of the line received the peremptory order to attack and take possession of the burial ground and church of the city occupying an elevated position,

where the Russians had caused some great entrenchments to be thrown, protected by complete breast work. Notwithstanding these apparently insurmountable obstacles, the orders given were obeyed with alacrity the colours moved steadily ; the attack was severe, the natural impetuosity of the French overcame everything, hut at an enormous sacrifice of þÿlife the regiment lost 500 men, and about 15 officers killed or wounded, almost all by the bayonet. Whilst the regiment was ascending to the assault of the burial ground, the Eagle which proudly led its van, and which had only been restored three months previous, was shattered by the grape shot which poured from the Russian cannon, and buried amidst the snow which covered that ensanguined field. The staff alone remained in the hands of the standard-bearers. The regiment, notwithstanding success, remained as if panic striken at an accident which recalled its former disgrace. But on the day following the murderous þÿcontest one of the severest of the campaign þÿ an officer oti going over the ground discovered that the snow liad disappeared, and was able to recover the wings of the Eagle, which was immediately restored to the staff, ana afterwards proved the rallying point until the battle of Wagram. On that day, the 4th performed prodigies of valour ; having overthrown the centre ol the Austrian line, it found itself immediately abreast a secdhd line, consisting of Hungarian Grenadiers, with which a bloody struggle commenced at the point of the bayonet. In
the short space of thirty minutes it lost 1600 men, all

the superior officers were either killed or wounded þÿ eight captains and fifteen lieutenants remained in that battle field, and the remnant of that noble regiment, on being called to muster next day , consisted only of a Captain-General. Such is the valour and heroic sell-devotion with which a French regiment loses its Eagle.

Intelligence from Havana. þÿ We have received by the Cherokee our files of El Diario de la Marino and la Gaceta de la Habana, to the 14th inst. The political news is of little interest. The Island, under the administration of the new Governor General, enjoys the most perfect tranquillity. The inhabitants have no more fears of the invasion, so much talked of. The papers of Havana daily publish official documents and decrees ordered by the administration. We give the two most interesting for the progress of that beautiful island : þÿ His Excellency the Governor General has ordered the publication of the concession made to companies for the establishment of electric telegraphs through all points, and to the principal cities of Cuba. The lines several small towns in their way ; from Union crossing will be established from Villanueva to Union, to Matanzas, from Buerbua to Macagua, from Tinguaro to Jacaro, from Navagas to Isabel, from San Felipe to Batabano, and from Rincmi to Guanajay, by San Antonio. The companies will be obliged to commence the works six months after the date of the concession, and to etablish them with the most possible activity. The second official document is from Queen Isabel, in which it is resolved, that the engines for the fabrication of sugar in the Islands of Cuba and Puerto Rico, shall be subjected, from the day of this royal decree, to the same common right. As for the engines existing already, they will be subjected to the same duty which they have paid, to the 1st of January, 1865, at
the end of the last term of the treaty. þÿ New York Herald, June 21.

New York Weekly Herald , June 13, 1852. Circular addressed by the California Chinamen to their Countrymen. From the San Francisco Herald, May 16. The splendid clipper ship Invincible sails this morning for Hong Kong. We understand she takes a number of circulars, addressed by the leading and most intelligent Chinamen in this State to their countrymen at home, advising them of the prejudices that have lately sprung up here against them ; of the severe measures which have been adopted throughout the interior to drive them from the mines, and warning them to cease emigrating to California, as they will no longer be welcomed. As this circular emanates from men high in authority and influence among the Chinese, it is expected that it will have the desired effect, and prevent any further increase for the present of our Asiatic population. At the same time it is not improbable that, vexed by the treatment their people have received in our mines, they will make such representation that retaliatory measures will be adopted by the Chinese government against Americans residing and trading in China.

The Chinese Emigration. From the Alia California, May 16 As this subject has much engaged the public attention of lale, a friend of ours (S. E. Woodworth, Esq ), has taken the pains lo collect the annexed statistics of arrivals and departures of Chinese emigrants. The gentleman named was for some time acting agent and consul for the Chinese in California, and the figures which he has furnished us may therefore be relied upon as quite correct. The first Chinese emigrants to California arrived in the brig Eagle, from Hong Kong, in the month of Februnry, 1848 þÿ two men and one woman But four arrived during the succeeding twelve months. On the first of February. 1849, there were but fifty-four Chinamen and one Chinese woman in California. On the first January, 1850, there were in California seven hundred and eightynine men and two women Ouiing the early part of that year, about three hundred Chinamen left here tor the Chincha Islands, having been engaged here by the Guano Company. On the 1st of January, 1851, there were in California 4,018 men and 7 women. On the 1st of January. 1852, there were 7 520 It is impossible to keep a perfect record of the deaths of Chinamen in this country, as they are scattered throughout the whole mining region, and very little correspondence is kept up between the different parties. There are doubtless many Chinamen in California not herein enumerated, whose numbers have never been reported at the Custom House, most of whom, however, con-

sist of cooks, stewards, crews, &c , of vessels from China, who have deserted while king in this port. Many also have returned to China or left California for other ports in like capacities Such arrivals and departures have been estimated to very nearly balance each other ; and as there are no means of ascertaining the number with correctness, they form no portion of the foregoing statement. It will be quite safe to set down the total Chinese population now resident in California at 12 000 and its increase will probably be frwrn 7,000 to 10,000 between this and the 1st January next. Under these circumstances we do not see any imperative necessity for the hue and cry which is attempted relative to this particular class of foreigners þÿ I he 1 rench and Spanish American population both exceed the Chinese very largely at the present moment, and no one fears danger or misfortune from their excessive numbers.

3 ST © IB D 2 51 AT! 3< Popular þÿDelusions. Men and women are credulous animals. Other animals are wary and suspicious in proportion as they are sagacious. But man, to whom alone reason is given, is distinguished by his credulity. Scarcely any theory is too absurd, any allegation too monstrous, any doctrines too se þÿIf contradictory, or any practices too ruinous and degrading, not to find a host of believers, with works according to their faith The worst consequences ol this credulity aresometimes entirely veiled fiom the world ; sometimes they take form and substance anddevelope themselves in organizations, associations, and special communities. Perhaps the most egregious credulity known at this day and here-about is that which places reliance upon the spirit rappings: and but few follies, of any day, have produced so much mischief. Ihis glaring imposture, for it is nothing else, has left in its course domestic misery, dethroned reason, desolation and death. Had we preserved all the instances of these evil resulis of the delusion which have met our eye in exchange papers, or otherwise come to our knowledge, and were here to classify them as above, the list would be positively appalling. Only yesterday, the following came to us in the St Louts Evening Despatch : þÿ A gentleman living in Illinois, and known to many in tiiis city, has a tanily ol sons and daughters, grown up men and women, of the highest respectability, Some vears ago Ins wile died, and he, living in the strong remembrance of her love as a faithful, good

wife, has never married During her life they were very happy, perhaps less than the usual domestic vexations of married life attended them; not the first blush of a suspicion ever attached to her good name. But this has been swept away by the magnetic juggling of a medium, who has borne evidence from some departed spirit, that she, the good wife, the revered in memory was unfaithful to him through her whole career, and that the children, one and all, were illegitimate. Wholly under the influence of a conviction that spiritual agency is a fixed fact, the gentleman has disinherited his children as common bastards, and driven them from his heart. A wife's memory blasted, children's names dishonored in their life, a happy home made desolate, and a lather's closing eve of life rendered dreadful in its loneliness On what evidence? On nothing l'his morning the Filchburg News mentions the death ol a lady at Luenburg, under circumstances of such a nature as leave little doubt that her death was precipitated by a prediction ol certain spirit rappers that she would die wilhin a specified time Cases of mental derangement, induced by belief in the imposture, are all too numerous, while even high intellects have been tainted by its influence. Add to these the radical but specious infidelity which it has fostered and diffused, the mawkish transcendentalism which it has substituted for practical common sense, and the wild and blasphemous vagaries which it pawns upon the world as revelations, while

it repudiates the only and Divine revelation of the Gospel, and one's heart aches at the visions of moral pestilence walking at noonday. We may not lift the curtain from domestic circles, or we might tell of the practical duties of life neglected, of filial and fraternal harmony interrupted, of morbid curiosity and of wasted energies, of mind crouching before superstition, and of a super-sensitiveness that finds a supernatural agent in every sound and motion. þÿ Commercial Advertiser, June 19.

Harper 't Magazine for July, Not long since a young English merchant took his youthful wife with him to Hong- Kong, China, where the couple were visited by a wealthy Mandarin. The latter regarded the lady very attentively, and seemed to dwell with delight upon her movements. þÿ When she at length left the apartment, he said to the husband, in broken English (worse than broken China) : " What you give forthat wifey-wife yours?" " Oh," replied the husband, laughing at the singular error of his visitor, "two thousand dollars." This the merchant thought would appear to the Chinese rather a high figure ; but he was mistaken. " Well," said the Mandarin, taking out his book with an air of business, " s'pose you give her to me; 1 give you five thousand dollar 1" It is difficult to say whether the young merchant was more amazed than amused ; but the very grave and solemn air of the Chinaman convinced him that he was in sober earnest; and he was compelled, therefore, to refuse the offer with as much placidity as he could assume. The Mandarin, however, continued to press his bargain : ' 1 give you seven thousand dollar," said he : " You take 'em ?" The merchant, who had no previous notion of the value of the commodity which he had taken out with him, was compelled, at length to inform his visitor that Englishmen were not in the habit of selling their wives after thev once came in their possession þÿ an nssertion which the Chinaman was very slow to believe. The merchant afterward had a hearty laugh with his young and pretty wife,

and told her thai he had just discovered her full value, as he had that moment been offered seven thousand dollars for her ; a very high figure, " as wives were going" in China at that time ! Nothing astonishes a Chinaman so much, who may chance to visit our merchants at Hong-Kong, as the deference which is paid bv our countrymen to their ladies, and the position which the latter sre permitted to hold in society. The very servants express their disgust at seeing American or English ladies permitted to sit at table with their lords, and wonder why men can so far forget their dignity 1

There is a certain London cockneyism that begins lo obtain among some persons even here þÿ and that is, the substitution of the word "gent." for gentleman. It is a gross vulgarism. In England, however, the terms are more distinctive, it seems. A waitingmaid at a provincial inn, on being asked how many "gents" there were in the house, replied, " Three gents and four gentlemen." " Why do you make a distinction, Betty 7" said her interrogator. "Oh, why, the gents are only hall gentlemen, people from the country. who come on horseback ; the others have their carriages, and are real gentlemen !"
